I have been using QB Pro with payroll (first basic, then enhanced) for years and have liked it a lot. This year, I am extremely unhappy with Intuit. Intuit has decided to not only charge their fee for payroll, which alone is actually fairly reasonable, especially if you get your payroll updated via Amazon, but now they have decided to tack on a $2 per month/per employee fee. A one-employee company won't be affected, apparently, but all employees above that first one will cost you $2 per month. If you have 11 employees (1st free, next 10 at $2/per month each), that is an extra $240 per year - for what? For absolutely nothing extra. You get no special benefit from this extra fee. You get nothing more than you got last year for your annual payroll fee that did not include this fee. $240 extra may not be much, but when it doubles the price (it more than doubles the price if purchased on Amazon, it is less than double if you buy directly from Intuit), it's a LOT. I am very unhappy with Intuit's decision to essentially rip off small companies with a decent number of employees. It's just wrong, and a sneaky way to substantially increase its prices (which have already increased substantially over the years). Shame on you, Intuit.

It is also frustratingly difficult to send multiple items to one customer in a single e-mail. I still have not found a way to send a statement and an invoice or two to one customer in a single e-mail. I am also still trying to figure out how to send multiple invoices to one client in one e-mail (a solution posted by Intuit still sent the two invoices in two separate e-mails to the client, though it seemed like they would be sent in the same e-mail), but you cannot copy and paste information into the e-mail form - you literally have to type out EVERYTHING you want included in the e-mail, including your own signature block. Very annoying.

It is overall a good program, though with some major flaws that really shouldhave been worked out by now (this program has been around a long time and is updated every single year), but the payroll aspect is becoming prohibitively expensive for small businesses.

I even tried rebooting and downloading directly from hrblock.com, but it always seemed to get stuck. I actually started a "chat" session from H&R Block's web site hoping to get some advice on how to get the update unstuck. After 15 minutes of waiting in the chat window for my turn to come, I remembered that the last update was still running. When I switched over to look at it -- amazingly, it finished! Apparently it just takes a very long time. So my suggestion for Mac users is: after you start the update, go get some lunch.

After the update, I did two returns, and the software is pretty much the same as in previous years. It's OK for simple returns, but there are several quirks. Here are this year's annoyances:

1) Ridiculously long update process described above.
2) It didn't ask for 1099-INTs even though I started both returns by importing last year's returns, which had 1099-INTs. You have to use the "take me to" menu to get to the right page and enter these.
3) Because it rounds all values to the nearest dollar, it creates some annoying audit messages. For example, say you enter a W2 where the state tax or CASDI or other amount was $0.37. It rounds to $0, which causes an audit error. You end-up having to delete the entry (e.g., CASDI) to get rid of the audit error.
4) If you import a previous year's return, it may include forms you don't need in the current year that cause audit errors. Example: you did some contract work in the previous year and entered some car mileage but had no mileage this year.
5) It annoys me every year that H&R Block offers free Federal e-file, but e-filing the State costs more than the software itself! Kind of a bait-and-switch scheme. I always just print the state return on paper and mail it.

Using the software is still easier than doing taxes by hand. If they fixed a few things, I'd rate it higher.

I was basically happy with Quicken 98 and Quicken 2000, but recent versions have been little more than a tweaking (or breaking) of the existing user interface and features. Every three years I have updated out of necessity because my investment updates stop working. Every time I ask Quicken the same question and receive the same answer. The only way to \\"subscribe\\" to the investment update service is to buy the current version of the program.

Quicken 2012 is noticeably slower than Quicken 2010, and more difficult to use because of the menu rearrangement and renaming of traditional buttons. For example \\"Enter\\" is now \\"Save\\". Some people obviously like the changes, but they hardly justify the price of a completely new version.

Still glaringly absent from the program is any way to adjust the font size of non-register text, or the size of the other display elements. As displays increase in resolution, the dots-per-inch scaling of Quicken has not been changed, nor has the user been given any option to set that. I am now 51 years old and I am finding things more difficult to see in Quicken. If you have vision problems, Quicken may not be for you. Yes, I know all the tricks for changing the DPI of the Windows desktop, but Vista and Windows 7 allowed programs to be \\"DPI aware\\", so why isn't Quicken? Windows 8 could be a real problem for Quicken because it departs even more radically from the traditional 96 DPI scaling. I don't recommend buying Quicken 2012 with any expectation of using it on Windows 8 and later.

The investment register still behaves completely different from the other registers, and appears to be grafted onto the program as an afterthought. For example, if I change the date sorting order, the dialog jumps to the oldest date, no matter which order I choose, or which item I had selected. Entering the price, shares and total price of a stock transaction requires me to click or press enter twice. Once to re-calculate something I already entered (of the three) and another to actually enter the data in the register.

The file name dialogs still do not remember previous folder paths well, and the reports annoyingly insist on tacking a 1, 2, 3, etc. on the end of report names. The features that have been added to the program over the years, all use a slightly different style of dialog boxes and options, making a complex process for navigating through the program. Some things require going through three or four menus or buttons. A great example of that is updating the price history of a stock.

In short, it seems that nothing but cosmetic changes have been made, and all the previous shortcomings have remained. I notice that the \\"one-step-update\\" still takes three mouse clicks to perform. When I check the box for \\"Show this dialog only if there is an error\\", the extra dialog box still always displays when there is no error.

PDF is an acronym for \\"Portable Document Format\\" created by Adobe in 1993. It is a file format for documents which enables the documents to viewed on many different kinds of hardware, software, and operating systems. Adobe has been the main vendor for PDF applications. The Adobe Reader has always been free, and that in large part has made the format one of the most popular standards on modern computes. However Acrobat, Adobe's PDF creator software is too expensive for most who would use it only for personal projects.

PDF Fusion by Corel fills a need that Adobe has not by providing a comparable application that is priced right for individuals. Even large businesses could benefit from the product and save a lot of money by opting for this product instead.

The software has all of the features that you would expect for creating PDF software. It has the ability to convert files directly from standard document formats like Word, PowerPoint, and Excel into PDF versions, plus the ability to open and edit existing PDF files. If you have an application that does not produce a standard format document, but it is able to print, you can select the PDF printer that is installed with PDF Fusion just like you would select a regular printer, and create a PDF file like that. This means that any application that has a printing capability can create PDF documents using PDF Fusion.

There many other features that make this a great product. You can password protect sensitive documents, so only those who know the password can open them. Documents can be signed to prove the document's source. Pages can be rearranged, rotated, added, and deleted. And so on.

For about 1/3 of the price for Adobe's lowest cost Acrobat version, you can get Corel's PDF Fusion. There are other solutions, even some that are free, but Corel's reputation as a great software producer will give you the peace of mind that you are getting a solid product.

I \\"upgraded\\" to Quicken Premier 2014 from an old version of Microsoft Money. Microsoft Money had been getting a little sluggish performing certain transactions and I started to worry that my extensive 12+ years of MS Money's historical data was getting to be a bit much for this aging program. And I was enamored by the idea of downloading data directly from my banks (a feature that Microsoft disabled when they removed support for MS Money) instead of entering it by hand. So at the end of last year I decided it was time to make the change.

I first tried GnuCash, but it did not do a good job of importing all of the old historical records from MS Money, and it was a bit more complicated to use than I liked. I also tried Mint, but I want the ability to be able to do everything I need to when offline. I thought Quicken would give me a good mix of online and offline use, so I \\"bit the bullet\\" and purchased the product.

Quicken did a much better job importing my MS Money data than GnuCash, though it was not a simple or straightforward process. There were enough incompatible fields and incorrect assumptions that Quicken made about the MS Money data that it took me a good two full days of work to get my accounts in Quicken to match reality. But I figured it was just a conversion issue, and once I got converted it would be smooth sailing, right? Wrong!

Quite simply put, I have found Quicken to be incredibly buggy and poorly written. For example, Quicken responds very slowly to simple tasks like re-sizing a window. A simple click-and-drag to resize Quicken's window takes about 4 seconds on my 3.00 GHz AMD Athelon II PC. Every other program on my computer performs window resizing as quickly as I can move the mouse. Another problem is that the software makes stupid assumptions in attempting to match downloaded transactions, even refusing to allow me to manually match a transaction with the exact same date and dollar amount, but insteadforces me to either enter a new (duplicate) transaction or choose one that happened a year ago. But most disconcerting of all, Quicken seems to mysteriously lose transactions that I have entered. Sometimes they will magically reappear minutes or hours later, (usually beside the two or three retries I had at the same transaction that also disappeared) but sometimes they just disappear completely and I have to enter them again.

It's not like I am completely inept at computers or accounting: I graduated with a major in Computer Information Systems and a minor in Business and have performed computer support for an accounting organization for many years. It's just that Quicken is that bad. If I have this many problems, I can't imagine how horrible this software is for the average person to use.

If you are thinking of using Quicken, I would recommend you try every other possible alternative first, and only use Quicken as the very last resort.

I downloaded the trial version of Elements 13 to see if it was worth purchasing the key code and upgrading my Version 12. Here's what I found out.

Adobe Photoshop Elements latest revision has a few changes, including improvements to the Help (which is no help in the previous versions--you are essentially combing the Web for what you want to do.) But is it worth upgrading if you have Version 12?

Help: ELive gives you some selected methods for removing \\"pet eye\\", editing batches of photos, using Facebook and some other frequently desired tasks. There are three new Guided Edits for black-and-white procesesing. There is an improved method to cut out and merge people or things from one photo to another. (Photomerge Compose.)
The Organizer has been changed a bit, to give it a look similar to many online image organizers--you can adjust the thumbnail view of your image as you scroll through them in the Organizer.

As usual, Photoshop Elements is a large program and somewhat slow. I reviewed Corel Paintshop Pro XL earlier and the difference in the amount of disk space they take up is astonishing: Photoshop Elements uses 3.5 gigabytes of disk space while Corel's PaintShop only uses 200 Megabytes (that's a lot smaller.) I found the Corel program was a lot faster to load and use.

The actually changes to version 13 are \\"under the hood\\" and not as visible to the average user: Elements 13 now supports high-DPI displays. It also is fully a 64-bit edition that allows the use of more than 4GB of RAM for heavy editing tasks. The average user will probably not have viewed this as a limitation in the past.

So should you upgrade? Unless you have had a problem with large edits in the past, I'd say if you have Version 12, this is not worth the upgrade. If you have upgraded your PC system recently and have an older version (11 and back) then yes, this is worthwhile.

I now have to contend with foreign assets and schedule K-1s and it's clear that H&R Block has been rather complacent in updating this software. Making matters worse, I sprang for the Premium edition this year thinking it would help me with the more complex items in my return, and it has failed.  The software does not support submission of form 8938 if you have more than 2 foreign assets to report. I could understand this as a one-time miscue in a year that the IRS dropped a bomb with little notice, but tax advisors should have been well aware of this reporting requirement a decade ago. I'll grant that it is probably a fraction of US filers at large that need to post more than 2 assets, but I understand competitive packages such as TaxACT and TurboTax both support continuation pages on the 8938. If you search the Internet for help on this issue, H&R Block doesn't have a fix yet and it appears you must inelegantly send a manual paper submission to the IRS, defeating one of the main reasons for buying software like this in the first place.  The Schedule K-1 support is also lacking. While there is a section for the form, it provides little guidance on the more complex items like lines where the K-1 has STMT and you have to look at supplementary documentation to determine the entry.   Ultimately I cannot recommend this software for anyone with more complex returns.   Adding insult to injury, Amazon doesn't allow refunds of digital purchases. I'm bending over for the IRS, now Amazon and H&R Block are getting in on the action too, and no one has any Vaseline. Thanks a lot guys.

Here are the steps we followed.
Our Use Case: The PC already have 2013 QuickBooks Pro + Enhanced Payroll 2013 (bundle purchased from Costco) running for past 1 year. 2013 Payroll subscription expired on March 20 2014. We wanted to purchase Enhanced Payroll 2014 from Amazon for $199 instead of paying Intuit $365 to extend the payroll subscription by another year.
How to do it:
1. Purchase Enhanced Payroll 2014 from Amazon. We selected \\"PC Download\\" option. Amazon would give you License Number and Product Number. That's ALL you need.
2. Go to your PC, Open QuickBooks Pro 2013.
3. Go to EMPLOYEES -> MY PAYROLL SERVICE -> MANAGE SERVICE KEYS/Payroll Subscription. You have to delete the \\"Enhanced Payroll 2013\\" subscription. Select \\"Enhanced Payroll 2013\\" and click \\"Remove\\".
We were worried that it will delete all previous payroll data. However it DOES NOT delete the previous payroll data; so no worries.
4. Now your QuickBooks Pro 2013 thinks that there is no active Payroll service for your account. This is what you need for the next step.
5. Go to EMPLOYEES -> Payroll -> \\"Install Payroll from Box\\" option.
6. Follow the on screen instructions and enter the Amazon provided License Number, Product Number, your credit card info. Next it will also ask you to login to Intuit. Use your \\"email id\\" and \\"password\\" you already created with Intuit. Complete the activation process.
7. That's it. You are all done. No need to call and spend 1 hour with Intuit customer support helpline.

Originally tried out the 30-day trial.  Used it to do some editing on a low-budget feature 4K movie that was done with RED cameras (R3D video file format). I had never used this editor before and the learning curve was very steep.  The so-called manual Adobe supplies is a great 400+ page sales brochure but it lacked details; all it really does it tell you what it is capable of doing but not the how's.  There is a lot of stuff that I figured out by intuition and trial and error and a lot of things I never did figure out how to get to work, in spite of slogging through the terabytes of Adobe postings and tutorials.  Searches for specifics rarely brought up anything useful. Also I hate the video tutorials since at the beginning they appear to be what I am looking for but I have to endure most of the tutorial just to find out that it isn't at all what I was looking for. Adobe really needs to work on their documentation. A lot.  A note to anyone that wants to use this editor for editing feature length movies:  Make sure you have a medium to high end computer with a high end graphics processor. I have a HP Phoenix box Windows 8.1 Pro with a 4-core i7 @ 3.2GHz, 16GB RAM, 4 TB HDD storage and 6TB USB3 external storage. Dual monitors with DVI. That part was fine but the graphics card is a GeForce GT640 with 2GB RAM (probably only cost about $100). The USB3 is a bit slow but okay (but keep your cables short !). This GT640 graphics card is the real bottleneck - Rendering was REALLY slow - we're talking 12 hours - start it up in the afternoon and come back in the morning and hope it didn't crash.  Need a much faster graphics card to get it down to 2-3 hours.  Another thing I encountered was the 2013 edition failed to load or run on my rig with Windows 8 but the 2014 edition works fine.  Addendum: switched to a Sapphire Radeon R9 270X 4GB GDDR5 and have it cranked up.  It is now around 2 hours to make a H.264 1920x1080 rendering of a 107 minute feature.  Make sure you have a 500-watt power supply, minimum, in order to use the board.  Recommend "An Editor's Guide to Adobe Premiere Pro" as a learning tool. It was written for Premiere Pro CS6 but most of the material is still quite useful.  Yet-another addendum: I have since finished my part of editing the feature and have uninstalled Premiere since it is still, in my opinion, difficult to learn and use.  Regardless, I can see that it does have a lot of nice features, some of which do not exist on any other similar editor (such as using markers to sync video and sound, for example). I'm sure that with the proper training, probably 3 months worth, I would be able to use it skillfully. However, I only had 3 months to do the edit so I had no choice.   Also, and not related to Premiere, I have removed the Sapphire Radeon R9 270X due to hardware/software conflicts: I suspect that there are resource conflicts since once the board was installed, my second internal DVD burner stopped working and the internal SD card reader stopped working. Once I removed this Sapphire card and put back the GeForce GT640, everything went back to normal. Also, this card has  a hardware problem related to the video RAM (intermittently unstable with either jumping displays or complete loss of sync).

The download was quick and easy, kind of a no brainer. When I went to update the software things went smoothly. Adding acounts appeared to be fairly straight-forward. Then I ran into a couple of snags. Quicken 2014 does not interface with TX HIgher Education Coord Board; TX Board changed their login method to a username, password, and date of birth. Quicken 2014 did not change their interface to reflect login changes. I then went to enter a manual loan but had a number of issues there, one of which dealt with the interest rate and period of interest compounding. I ended up deleting the manual loans since it threw off calculations in other items, ie Net Worth or interest paid over time period X, to name two issues.

The next set of issues I encountered dealt with budget numbers, imported account information , and poor performance, deserves a separate paragraph. Our budget numbers kept getting thrown off and could not figure out why. It turns out that info in the cloud was not getting synced correctly which resulted in numbers changing on a regular basis; I ended up deleting the info on the cloud. Once i deleted it and then performed a one-step update, I was able to sync my info, hoping it stays in sync with laptop, cloud, and cell phones. Our imported account information on one checking account showed a negative balance in the All Accounts transactions fields despite having a correct amount listed in the account itself within Quicken and online at the bank web-site. I deleted that account and set it back up in Quicken to resolve the issue. Speaking of the bank account with the update issue, there have been a couple of problems with the password being invalid or not viable, hoping that the delete of the account and resync of cloud date resolves this issue.

Performance...poor performance..lack of performance. I have noticed where Quicken would hang, you could not close the application or get it to do anything other than show a screen with strange characters and remnants of data you had been entering. Luckily enough forcing the application closed in the task manager helped to resolve the issue with no data loss. I noticed that the performance issue happened when I was editing our budget with rollover options. When selecting the rollover balances at the end of each month, the application itself was slow to respond then would hang. What I ended up doing was adding rollover balances to a several items and then closing out of the application on a regular basis One other issue with performance happened when editing the budget itself and choosing categories to display; it was painfully slow to watch the screen redraw and the mouse being sluggish, but trudged thru that one. My machine is not fast by any means and does not have a lot of RAM compared to machines coming out today. It has a Intel Duo Core 2.4 Ghz, 4 GB RAM, 7200 RPM 150 GB HD, and Win 7 64-bit. Quicken hardware recommendations will not run this application. (If you believe that a machine with their minimum requirements will run the application to where it isusable then let me know. I may just buy you a copy of Quicken 2014 Home for your very own.)

BOTTOM LINE: I like the application and various features. I also like troubleshooting hardware and software issues, in the IT industry. However, I don't appreciate all of the issues I have had so far since I am not paid to troubleshoot their software. In my opinion I don't think this software is meant for everyone. A lot of banks and credit card companies now offer a variety of features that Quicken does; if you have everything consolidated to one or two banks, consider using their services. I am giving this product a two star rating because of the issues mentioned above and will try to update everyone in 3-4 months on additional thoughts or issues.

Last year, I had prepared the tax returns on an XP system and this year, I was working on a new Windows 7 system with just the 2014 tax software loaded. So, after an hour on Chat, I was told to load the 2013 software, open and resave the prior year tax return and then I should be able to import it into the 2014 tax software. So, I went back to the 2013 software -- used the RESTORE feature and followed the steps below. Voila, my prior year tax data and ALL my depreciation info hasbeen imported into the 2014 business tax software.
Need to load prior year tax software ie. H&R Block 2013
Need to RESTORE atx file. This option is under the “File” tab.
Once file restored, need to re-save tax return in H&R Block 2013
Then Open current year tax software ie H&R Block 2014.
Import the restored saved tax return from H&R Block 2013
File should now work in 2014 software.

Complaining is easy to do, so in order to provide you with as objective a review as possible, I'm going to start with what I like about this software. I love Quicken. I've been using it since 2006 and my father (who introduced me to the product) has been using it for decades. What Quicken has always lacked is a substantial budgeting component. That issue is finally addressed in 2013 and it works reasonably well! However, those who added this feature likely aren't that familiar with personal budgeting themselves, as the system they set up is clunky at best and not very intuitive. However, we have gotten it to work for ourselves and our budget and now we couldn't be happier!

The real shame with this product is its mobile app. Finally releasing a mobile version of Quicken was what convinced me to upgrade to 2013 from 2012. Given the complex record-keeping that Quicken itself does, an app that is simply a companion to the desktop version (instead of a replacement) is understandable, especially when one considers Intuit's ownership of Mint.com. However, what is not understandable is why Quicken released this mobile app with such little development. It looks pretty, but has failed in two different ways for me since purchasing 2013 (two weeks ago!). I understand that bugs can occur in commercial software, but for me as an individual user to experience two separate bugs in the syncing and mobile features in two weeks is unacceptable. The most unfortunate part is Quicken's technical support staff, who are either utterly unhelpful (perhaps due to a lack of experience with the software themselves) or condescending. The online forum staff are more knowledgable, but it seems like they themselves are kept in the dark often on the inner workings of the online components of Quicken.

All in all, this is a great product but unfortunately the new features have a steep learning curve for the average user. If any computer software reviewer sites out there are reading this, here is my suggestion: Publish a step-by-step guide for how to budget in Quicken. Include checking to make sure the budget is zero-sum and how to use Savings Goals in tandem with the budget itself.

One last warning to fellow users: it appears that the budgets are saved in the Quicken Cloud, NOT your desktop. That means that, should something go wrong with your online account that requires its deletion and re-creation, you will find that your budget has disappeared. Make sure you record your final budget in a second form (i.e. a spreadsheet) to make sure that you don't lose that info if the unfortunate were to occur!

To begin - I have an MBA in finance and offer financial planning advice for a living.  I used quicken 2004 for a number of years, and switched to mint.com a few years back.  Unfortunately many users of Mint.com suffered some issues when Mint.com made some integration updates, esentially loosing some historical information.  Thinking you get what you pay for (Free) I thought that I would buy quicken premier.  I have had several major issues with quicken 2012 premier.  They are:  1)  It is very ackward to enter in a loan payment for a mortgage.  I didn't even see a place where this could be scheduled.  You must enter loan payments in a specific fashion for the interest in principal to calculate correctly.    2)  Loan payments are duplicated - as you must enter them manually - then they are downloaded (without the necessary interest and principal data) and then must be deleted.  3)  Automatic data downloads.  A major financial institution worked correctly for Mint.com, but did not work for quicken 2012.  I asked quicken, and they said that they are different products and too bad.  4)  Budgeting.  Basically, the budgeting segment of Quicken 2012 does not work.  The software advertises some eye candy graphs for budgeting, but the data does not flow through correctly.  I had a mysterious and large \\"un-catagorized\\" spending item show up on the budget.  When I would look at all my transactions to see which ones did not have a catagory assigned to them, I found none.  Secondly, sub-catagories do not roll up into main catagories.  I created two budgets thinking that I must have done something wrong.  The charts on the screen had problems updating to show the correct budget.  I saw no way of removing an account from the budgeting function.  Suppose you sell a mutual fund in your 401-K for a loss - when you look at your budget, your income will be less than your paychecks because quicken is counting the loss on a transaction.  If you look at the online help forums, they are full of people complaining about this and other problems.  Further, when \\"chatting\\" with support people, they basically acknowledge that there are REAL bugs in the software, and that certain functions do not work - like the budgeting.  Here is my take:  Intuit is trying to make quicken a non-cloud version of mint.com with a few extra features.  This is their first time adding in many of the mint.com - like features and they actually failed making functional software.  My guess is that they threw this together and did not test it.  Do yourself a favor and wait a few years before buying a quicken product until they have things figured out.  I wish I would have saved myself the time.

I've used this software to add green screen effects for music videos and although there is an intial learning curve, the end results are quite impressive.

In particular, I like the chroma key and customized motion options.

The chroma key option allows knocking out green screens or blue screens to layer videos in a way that people or objects in the videos can "interact" with other video images and backgrounds. Combined with customized motions, this allows me to move a picture or video by manually placing it where I want it to be during key frames of other videos or images. I've used this to add fire effects "attached" to certain objects, move people around the screen, simulate flying, walking up stairs in a picture (using green screen only), etc.

The only glitch I've found is that this customized motion works better with moving pictures than moving videos. When I move a video image around, I often get a thin dark gray border around the image and I cannot crop this dark border out. This is most noticable when the image has been chroma keyed and the dark border surronds a transparent area, and is even more apparent when the video image (and its dark border) is moving over a light colored background.

I've had less success with the motion tracking option, which I think would probably work better if you have a high contrast object (light object being tracked on a dark background or vice versa), so I stick with the customized motion.

There are a host of other effects, but I rarely use any of them except for the various text over screen transitions. You may like the other effects better if you're into color filters, distortions, and such. Keep in mind though that using a color or monocrome filter will mess up your chroma key, if you're using a green screen.

Overall, this is a nice amateur video production software, espcially for someone who can develop their own green screen images (or download them from youtube and other places on the web.

This is for the Macintosh version of TurboTax Deluxe 2011. I have used TurboTax (and MacinTax - the Mac version from the 1990's before they renamed it TurboTax) every year. Last year, I tried H&R Block's software, but quickly returned it and bought TurboTax. There is no equivalent to TurboTax on the market.

The Good: As usual, TurboTax is relatively error-free (as far as I could tell) and easy to use. One can use the walk-through step-by-step approach in which TurboTax leads you through everything step by step. Or, if one wants to just fill out the forms, one can go into forms mode and enter the information that way - a bit quicker since TurboTax does need to cover areas that are irrelevant to one's situation in the step-by=step method.

I purchased mine early so I could get a head start on my taxes. One can estimate figures (marking them for future review/correction) and can make itemized lists that are totaled up and entered in the appropriate blocks - great for listing the details of any figures added to the forms. When adding a state form, it is so quick and easy to fill out. One can file (I think) five or ten federal returns for free - great feature for a family of teenagers who work.

The description pretty much covers all of the capabilities. Hands down, this is a much better program than H&R Block, which was very buggy - itemized lists could not be modified, the right forms would not come up when selected...you can see the list of bugs in my evaluation of H&R Block's software last year (I have no reason to believe it will be any better this year).

Now, the Bad: I have only one complaint - pricing. The software is a bit expensive, but that is understandable since this is a very comprehensive and non-buggy program compared to the other one. But the ancillary costs are too much. The first state is free (with TurboTax Deluxe), but the others are $39.95 each. As a family that moved in the middle of last year, I needed two state packages. Also, to file the state forms, it costs $19.95 per state per return. So for my family, which includes three teenagers and a military move, it would cost me an extra $239.45 to file the returns (five people, two states plus the cost of downloading the second state). This is quite expensive, especially considering the minimal income that my teenagers received. The way around this, of course, is to print the state tax returns and mail them in. It still cost me $39.95 for the download of the second state, which I thought was a bit much since I already paid for TurboTax Deluxe, but it wasn't unpalatable. However, for $39.95, I would think the state return should be filed for free, not for an additional $19.95 per return. Changing Intuit's policy to provide free state e-files for the states that are purchased separately would be a reasonable and good business practice.

All in all, this is a very good program. I have been using it yearly since the 1990's. Every time I stray to a different company, I come running back to TurboTax. Save yourself the grief of poor quality, bug-ridden software and just stick to TurboTax.

I've been using TurboTax for years, but this year's experience made me realize it's time to stop doing my own taxes. The software worked fine for the most part, which is the reason for the relatively high rating. I do have a few complaints about the program itself that aren't specific to my personal situation. First, there continues to be an issue where any changes late in process to earlier steps can cause problems with the integrity of the entire form. Second, I don't understand why you can't use the SnapTax app to photograph your W-2s, then import them into the desktop version of TurboTax (this only works with the online version). Also, this year, one state disallowed a credit the software insisted I was entitled to claim.

The real issue I have is the cost of the entire undertaking. Only one state is included here; if you need to file in additional states, you pay almost as much for each one as the Federal + State + E-file edition costs (without the free e-file). I added this additional cost to the original price, plus the Audit Defense service (optional - the Intuit people gambled that many of their users would be fearful of messing up somewhere, a pretty safe bet in my case). I realized I could employ a CPA for only a little bit more money (and a lot less hassle).

Bottom line: Ask yourself, "Are my taxes relatively straightforward?" Meaning you owe only in one state, have only a few W-2s/1099s, and have deductions that are typical (uniforms, very specific professional journals like JAMA, etc.) Then I would recommend TurboTax Deluxe without hesitation. For those with a more complicated tax situation, really consider whether it makes financial sense to continue to self-file.

I read the reviews here and thought I might offer a bit of balance. I transcode video from my digital cameras all the time... and over the years, as I've changed cameras, I've had several different video formats. The one that was the biggest problem was an old Kodak I owned in 2004. It shot video but at 12.9 frames per second... and I could not both merge these small files, resize, AND up the framerate to 25 or 30 fps. This program lets me do this.

I only use h264 to encode... so I can't speak for any of the other codecs... and this program does have all the advanced settings... but it documentation is terrible and unlike some very capable free programs I've used like AVI4PSP, AVIDEMUX, and Handbrake... you can't run a cursor over a setting and get some guidance to learn what it does and many of these settings give you no preset values to choose from. That's just crazy.

As for the person who got worst results than what they put in... I can only guess they don't know what their doing... and picked a bitrate way too low for good results. It's always best to do at least a 2pass encode with a adequate bitrate for the format. So for standard 640x480 30fps I use 1800-2000kbs. That's still way lower than the 9000kbs my camera shoots at.. but then it uses an very inefficient format.

That being said... it's not worth $49. It doesn't even give that as the regular price at their site. There it's $29.

Avast! is the AV on both of my computers at home, and I have installed it on about a dozen friends' computer to whom I provide tech support. I've used it for at least 5 years, starting with the replacement of my former AV, Avira AntiVir, which ceased to automatically update the virus pattern files (couldn't fix it). Avast's anti-virus capabilities are impressive; I haven't had a virus for the entire 5 years. I can only recall finding a few spyware programs or trojans on my computers during that time. They were discovered and removed by Malwarebytes, which I also have on all computers. I don't downgrade Avast! for letting those thru because its focus is on viruses, not other malware forms.

The problem with Avast! is similar to that of other software manufacturers: They feel the need to constantly change the interface so you feel like you're getting a new-and-improved product -- along the lines of Microsoft's horrendous changes from Windows 7 to Windows 8. In that process, items that used to be easy to find no longer are, and they're in strange places. For example, to find the place where you can set the longevity of pop-ups (like the one that tells you your virus definitions have been updated) or configure sounds are now under the subheading of "Appearance". Would you ever think that that subheading would contain the settings for pop-up time and sounds?? They used to be under subheadings for "Pop-ups" and "Sound".

Second, with the advent of the latest version, you now frequently receive pop-ups over which you have no control trying to sell you pay-for updates or other products. They're annoying. Perhaps you don't get those if you have the paid version, I don't know. And like so many Microsoft products, new versions can contain FEWER features than previous versions. For example, older free versions had a "Sandbox", where you could evaluate suspicious programs in a virtual window to keep them from doing any harm toyour computer. That now comes only with the paid version.

Despite these shortcomings, I would still recommend Avast! because of its strong AV capabilities. But if the interface and/or annoying pop-ups get worse, I will consider changing to another AV.

Microsoft Word 2013 is a classic example of bad 'feature creep.' I do a lot of writing and yet this word processor is full of things that seemingly want you to be unproductive. If you've read enough of the reviews then you have probably seen most of the issues. I'll throw in a few more: there's only three color options. Previous MSWord's had options to help alleviate the eyes by changing up the background - the area upon which rests the 'page' itself. Word 2013 has a whopping three options: blinding white (the default setting, where you can hardly even see the page you're working on as it blends into the background, genius!), a less blinding white (they call this one grey), and a timid grey color (they call this one dark grey).

First off, it's 2014. Why are there only three options? Are you telling me a giant corporation like Microsoft couldn't swing more than that? It's insanely lazy. Second, who in their right mind would put a white-page on a white-background as the default setting? Thirdly, why are all the backgrounds SOLID? It's so completely unnatural to have the blank space behind the page be a monochrome color, because no matter what you're going to end up with a blank white space resting upon a solid color which is way too strong of a juxtaposition. Awful, AWFUL design.

Another issue of 'feature creep' is the damn animations of the cursor. When you type, the cursor 'animates' instead of jumps forward. This means that if you're a fast typer like me - well over 100+ WPM - then the cursor is LAGGING behind, being swallowed up in the words being put on the page. I can't help but shake my head at how utterly dumb this is. Why is this a feature? It only serves to be distracting. Was there some issue with the previous cursor's ability to just be on the page? Do we live in a world where everything has to be moving at all times? It gets even more eye-rolling when you jump to the next paragraph and you get to watch the cursor drag itself over instead of just jumping down. If you go back and forth enough, like I sometimes do since I write so fast but need to make amends, then the cursor is lolly gagging back and forth instead of juts doing its damn job. WHO THE HELL DESIGNS THIS CRAP?

And speaking of all-caps, Word 2013 used to keep your titles in capitalized letters. That one they did fix, but it just goes to show you how utterly stupid this program's design is. I haven't even scratched the surface of other issues, but they are there. It's just that in addition to those these little things like a blinding color scheme, terrible aesthetic design, and a bizarrely introduced animated cursor only help fuel the fire. As someone who has to do a lot of writing, I plan on never, ever buying another Word from Microsoft again. I use word processors to WORK, not be dazzled, and I don't want to look away from the computer with blinded eyes because the wizkids at Microsoft don't know the first thing about design.

1/5 at best. If you just want a word processor, there is no reason to upgrade to Word 2013.

I have used Quicken for 20 years now, and upgrade versions every year. Upgrades always went well until the move from 2009 to 2010, and they've been getting worse every year. Upgrade to 2013 is no exception.

The worst part about all of this is that when you upgrade, your data is converted -- so there is no going back. Don't tell me about backups -- I backup my data to 9 different hard drives every time I make a change to my Quicken data file. The issue is that the data is converted, and no longer backward-compatible, so once you have converted -- and then commence to make any additions to your data -- there is just no going back (unless, of course, you keep an older version running on a different computer, and replicate EVERY transaction in both versions in parallel -- how long you think that'll work and keep them both accurate?).

Anyway, when I upgraded from 2009 to 2010, all 42 of my online repeating payments got screwed up. Quicken's solution -- delete them all, and re-enter them. Note that that required deleting and re-entering in BOTH Quicken and the bank, since 2010 would not download the existing repeating transactions from the bank. Well -- it downloaded a few of them -- but -- would you trust that going forward? For the next 4 months after recreating all these transactions, I manually confirmed each and every one of them, each and every month, between the Quicken screen and the bank's screen, to be sure they were working, that the payments had happened, that I didn't end up with any late payments .......

Well, in the 2010 to 2011 upgrade -- guess what -- the same thing happened again. Another 4 months of manual confirmation after over 40 transactions were manually deleted and re-entered.

So -- along came 2013 upgrade. This time the repeating transactions actually transferred over, except now there are some that have expired (they were for a set time, the last payment has been made) -- and they won't disappear from my automatic payment listing. I CANNOT make them go away, I CANNOT delete them -- so now I am manually confirming every month that the bank is not sending multiple payments to the utility company, cable company, etc. There are a couple of \\"ghost\\" repeating online payments that do not show up in the scheduled transaction lists that regularly show up in my check register though -- so I have to confirm that those payments aren't real every month too.

Further, the reports function just simply does not work. The ad hoc reports produce garbage, don't include the right information, do include wrong information, selecting by category or account etc just doesn't filter the right data. The custom reports that I had set up and used for years, and which had survived the version upgrades successfully over the years -- did not survive the 2013 upgrade. I can't recreate them because the reports function in 2013 is just plain BROKEN. Back to Excel.

Transactions do not reliably download from the bank's website when the accounts are updated. Most do, but not all. Somehow other computers are not satisfied with being close -- at least not *my* credit card company. So, reconciling accounts is a major chore to ferret out the missing, and all too often duplicated, transactions that are found in the registers. Doing a \\"One Step Update\\" is always an adventure because the passwords stored in the password vault don't always work -- some do, some don't, never the same ones -- and evidently, sometimes they must hammer away at trying to get access so many times that I get locked out of the website for too many invalid attempts -- I don't find that out until I go to do a manual logon to a site that didn't download correctly, so I can then do a webconnect download, and find that I am locked out, and then have to go through a password reset process with that provider. Never happened until v2011, but was consistent in v2012. Still here in 2013.

When I called the bank about the downloaded transaction and online repeating payment issues, they pointed the finger at Quicken (and most probably rightly so) -- and forwarded me there. First thing Quicken did was ask for a credit card number in order to provide product support. It was going to cost me more for product support, for a brand new product that didn't work as advertised, than it cost to purchase the product in the first place. After calling that bluff (and I am sure being noted as a bad customer in the process), all the other horror stories about Quicken support were experienced as well -- no follow-up, no feedback, no success. English as a second language is a minor issue in this disaster.

So -- Quicken 2013 really becomes nothing more than a very pretty looking Excel spreadsheet for me -- a fancy check register -- because I no longer trust ANYTHING that it does. I manually confirm online payments that it sends -- repeating, one-time, or otherwise. I manually check my bank balances with the bank's webpage, because I do not trust that all transactions are accounted for, and therefore cannot trust the balance shown, nor the forecasted balance for the next 30/60 days.

What a great product this used to be. I've just never figured out how to live without it after relying on it for so long.

But -- as I find myself looking for ways to simplify my life, living without Quicken is beginning to enter those thoughts.

[[Third time posting this review - the previous posts have been mysteriously deleted, but the problems in Quicken 2014 remain. Perhaps Intuit pressures Amazon to remove negative reviews from "nonverified" buyers - I bought my copy at Costco.]]

As a loyal Quicken user since 1997, and one who buys the new version every year, I am astonished at how bad this new release is. The number of new usability problems introduced with Quicken Premier 2014 (on Windows 7) is so large that it seems clear the product was rushed to market to meet Intuit's annual new release (new revenue?) deadline without performing sufficient quality assurance. Below I will list the problems I have discovered so far, and I will update my review if and when any new interim releases resolve these problems.

KEYBOARD SHORTCUTS ARE BROKEN IN THE REGISTER VIEW. The Register view is the bread and butter of Quicken: this is where you enter and review transactions. Common functions such as cut, copy, and paste of text fields (Control-X, Control-C, and Control-P) do not work - I must use the mouse and select these functions from the Edit menu (which still lists the keyboard shortcuts). Similarly, Control-R does not bring up the Reconcile window, Control-J does not (always) bring up the Bill and Income Reminders window, Control-S does not bring up the Split Transaction window, Up-Arrow and Down-Arrow keys do not shift focus to adjacent transactions, etc. These problems are especially noticeable when switching to another application, then back to Quicken.

KEYBOARD FOCUS IS LOST IN THE REGISTER VIEW. If I highlight a text field such as Payee or Amount, then switch to another application and switch back to Quicken, the highlighted field is no longer active. This means I must use the mouse to re-select the field before I can begin typing a value. It's often the case that I will switch apps - for example, when reviewing a credit card statement and comparing transactions. This particular problem makes me think the name "Quicken" should be changed to "Slowen".

DOWNLOAD TRANSACTIONS / BILL AND INCOME REMINDERS PANE IS ~ALWAYS~ PRESENT. When switching to the Register view from one account to another account, this pane at the bottom of the view is always presented in maximized form, which minimizes the number of transactions I see in the Register. Previously, this pane only appeared when there were unprocessed downloaded transactions or active reminders for the account. It's annoying to have to close the view every time I switch between account registers to review or enter transactions. I can see 10 transactions (2-line display) with the pane closed, but only 3 transactions when the pane is open.

DOWNLOADED TRANSACTION RED FLAG. After One Step Update, Quicken shows a red flag for accounts with new transactions. Sometimes I will see the red flag, go to that account register, and find NO downloaded transactions (particularly for investment accounts). If I perform One Step Update again, or just select Update Transactions, sometimes the new transactions will appear as expected.

ONE STEP UPDATE FAILS CONSISTENTLY FOR SOME ACCOUNTS. I have seen numerous errors for Wells Fargo Bank and PayPal. I have disabled and re-enabled One Step Update for these accounts numerous times, with no improvement.

ATTACH RECEIPT TO TRANSACTION. I became a huge fan of this feature in the previous 2013 release. I could scan a paper receipt or document to a PDF file, attach that file to a transaction, and discard the receipt. After attaching the file, a Quicken window would display the receipt, providing instant confirmation that the correct file was attached. But in Quicken 2014, the attachment shows up only as a generic PDF icon. To verify the attached file, I must double-click the icon to open Adobe Reader. To view any existing attachment, I must click multiple times to bring up the external Adobe Reader. On the support chat rooms, Intuit says the new behavior is necessary to support attaching other file types such as photo images taken with smart phones. Really? This is the same Quicken product that uses a built-in (and very antiquated) web browser to navigate to the web sites of financial institutions (rather than simply launching your favorite browser). Can't they include a PDF and JPG viewer in the application?

As of October 16, 2014, I'm using the latest R7 version of Quicken Premier 2014 for Windows. As I stated at the top of this review, I'll update this review if and when any of these problems is resolved in an interim release. For the time being, avoid this release and stick with Quicken 2013 or earlier.

A recent upgrade to Windows 7 64-bit forced me to give up using MS Money 2000.  I had been using the old version on Money to manually track all my accounts.  My plan is to do the same with Quicken. Quicken uses ledger format with a record in one row.  I know this is traditional accounting format, but one plus to the old MS Money was that you can view your entry on a graphical layout that looks like a check or a deposit slip and it had tabs for credits, debits and transfers.  I find myself stumbling around the Quicken window trying to find basic functions.  For example Reconcile and Transfer Money are under the Account Actions button.  There's plenty of real estate for making popular functions their button.    Another silly grip is that when you reconcile, it does a window pop-up.  With my old MS Money, I could tile Money and my PDF statement to go through and reconcile the entries.  But since the reconcile page is pop-up you cannot arrange your windows to do a side-by-side or top and bottom.  I did use the function to download account data when initially configuring the program.  It contacted my credit union but failed to retrieve and records.  For my mainstream bank and credit card company it was somewhat more successful. For my credit card it somehow messed up the initial balance and showed a current balance that was way off. It took me a while review, and fix all my accounts from the data it downloaded.  This is why I am manually entering data as mentioned above.  That, plus I prefer to see payments to my credit card as post dated transfers and not have a several day discrepancy between to two accounts until the payment clears online.  On the positive side, I do like how the bills are shown in a graphical manner.  And the program does track your accounts.  Reports are interesting but probably not significantly useful for me.  But for a company who has been in the business of personal finance software for probably over 20 years, I am woefully unimpressed with the user interface.  Not sure how today's quicken compares with that of decade ago (online features aside) but one would think that would be enough input from consumers to evolve and efficient and affective interface.

I'm a long time Quicken user -- my file goes back to 1/1/1993. I've been using Quicken 2013 Home & Business since 2013. But, after not being able to download financial transactions from my brokerage firm for six months and unable to get any satisfactory help from either the financial institution or Quicken, I figured that as a last resort I would do this upgrade.    BIG MISTAKE!!!!! Not only is the transaction download still broken, but this version of Quicken crashes within 2-3 minutes of me loading it -- every time. No reason given, it just crashes. This isn't production worthy software. It's junk!!!! Amazon should pull this product and Quicken should be ashamed!!!    But for now, here is my review:    What's new (compared to my 2013 version - which is two versions back)    1) A new login mechanism that routes through their servers - not sure what the benefit really is. It's more different than useful. There are various notes in the UI which explain this feature, but on my computer, the text didn't fit in the text area assigned so it's clipped and you can't read the whole sentences.  2) A new ability to check your credit rating for free.  3) Lots and lots of crashes. This is a product released to a schedule and not a quality level. Shame on you Intuit! What I don't get is how they added so many bugs while changing so little -- that is really remarkable.    What's the same:    1) Pretty much everything else:    - An old fashioned late '90s era user interface that hasn't changed in years now.    - The spinning cursor everytime I enter a transaction -- it seems to have to really think about every single key click at times    - Underneath the covers I see prehistoric SGML code (that's 1980s era software technology from before the world wide web), gwbasic/qbasic (that's DOS era Microsoft BASIC), and bits of SOAP (early 2000s Internet technology). It's all pretty much obsolete code so the ugly Windows 95 era UI is actually a bit more modern than what's underneath.  2) So-so tired old customer support. If you can find it, you can get online support for free. They really hide what you must do to get it though. When you get through, it's friendly but not particularly helpful.    All in all, Quicken doesn't have any competition. They're a $4.2 billion company -- but they add a few (really few) bells and whistles each year, increment the version number, and ship the same old stuff and ask you to buy it all over again. It's an awful way to do business -- and I hope it's a way that will eventually end in Intuit's demise. They don't deserve our business.    UPDATE: I got my money back and have returned to Quicken 2013. I have another year before Intuit pulls the plug on that version and forces me to update.    WARNING: Pay close attention to the fact that a lot of the positive reviews (about 2/3 right now) are not coming from people who have verified purchases. Intuit seems to be encouraging their beta testers (I'm surprised they have any) to come on here and give glowing reviews to counter all the negative reviews from people who purchased the product.

There is no good personal finance package for a Mac.  I've tried iBank 5.5.3, GnuCash for Mac 2.6.6, Moneydance 2015.5, AceMoney 4.36.1, and now Quicken for Mac 2015.  Each is unsatisfactory in its own way.  This review applies to Quicken for Mac 2015 version 2.5.0, with some comments about comparable programs.  The best thing about Quicken for Mac is that export of Quicken Windows data (via a Windows-based add-on exporter) works reasonably well.  Not all data can be imported into the Quicken for Mac 2015, because it simply doesn't support the same feature set, but I'd rate the process as very good on the average.  The import process is almost as fast as Moneydance, much faster than GnuCash, and much, much faster than iBank (which takes many hours to import the same data that other programs import in minutes).  After import, Quicken for Mac balances are mostly accurate, which can't be said for some other programs.  Speaking of keeping account balances correct: The basic function of a personal finance package is to balance your checkbook and other accounts.  How hard could that be?  Well, much got lost in re-designing Quicken Windows into a Quicken for Mac; and "reconcile to online balance" and "reconcile shares" functionality is gone.  Instead, you get to manually enter starting and ending balance (from printed statements?), then reconcile transactions between those two dates -- only cash, not shares -- and that's even for online accounts downloaded by Quicken for Mac.  Unfortunately, that's not a quick way to balance your checkbook.  Why is a sensible reconciliation feature missing on the Mac version, while the Windows version has it?  It's a mystery, along with many other mysteries.  For example, Quicken for Mac can export transactions as .CSV, but then can't import its own exported .CSV file.  Who comes up with design specifications like that?  Another mystery: A brokerage account has a cash balance but, when asked, Quicken for Mac claims that the"Online Balance" is zero in the "Transactions" view -- yet shows it as "Available Cash" under the "Portfolio" view.  That's a bit schizophrenic.  Others have pointed out that Quicken for Mac falls short in many areas (particularly reporting), when compared to the Windows version.  However, the Windows version (running within a virtual PC on the fastest Mac) became excruciatingly slow over the years.  Every transaction edit results in ~5 seconds of internal updates before anything else can be done -- something is badly engineered in the Windows version.  Quicken for Mac (working on the same data) is quite responsive, perhaps thanks to internal improvements.  These are two very, very different programs, even though they both say "Quicken".  In summary, Quicken for Mac 2015 is not terrible, but it isn't very good either.  It works in a limited way, but some basics (like support for reconciling cash and shares to online balances) are not there, resulting in much manual labor compared to the Quicken for Windows.  On the positive side, Quicken for Mac is reasonably responsive, while Quicken for Windows became painfully slow (running within a virtual machine on even the fastest Mac).  Intuit needs to improve this program.  The competition isn't much better but others are gradually improving their offerings.  Update: Quicken for Mac (2015 or 2016) does not work with T. Rowe Price retirement accounts, although brokerage accounts should work.  TRP offers no solutions for this.  Also, as of late 2015, importing an .OFX or .QFX file downloaded from a bank which uses this method can fail, if Quicken for Mac decides that the financial institution has not signed up with Intuit. This is beyond bad.  Intuit has no business being in the middle of bank-customer data downloads.  This raises concerns about whether Intuit is aggregating information about Quicken users' financial connections, which creates a huge security vulnerability.  For this reason, I'm downgrading Quicken for Mac to only two stars.

I have an old copy of Microsoft 2002 and have been wanting to upgrade for years. I looked into the possibility of upgrading recently, but I read somewhere that your purchase is only good for one license on one PC, regardless of the length of time your PC lasts. Imagine the surprise encountered whenever a new customer decided to upgrade their PC or by anyone who experienced a hardware failure. I couldn't believe such a ridiculous policy applied to the general public. It might make sense for a business or corporate license, but the `average Joe' isn't going to read through licensing policies and legal jargon before buying an Office software package for home use. It seemed obvious to me at that point that Microsoft was trying to capitalize on the trust of the common home user, at the expense of their hard earned income. This severely damaged whatever trust I had for the company.

Fast-forward to just yesterday, when I decided to review my options, and I discovered Microsoft amended their policy to allow users to transfer their license from one computer to the next, provided the license is only active on one PC at a time. Great, I figured! So I proceeded to purchase the software, thinking Microsoft again had the customer's interests in mind.

I received the purchase confirmation email, clicked the URL provided, clicked the \\"Get Started\\" button on the Microsoft website, and it brought me to a Microsoft login screen. Apparently you have to create a Microsoft account in order to even access your software. Not a big deal or even an uncommon practice these days, but during the account creation process, if you inadvertently select the wrong birth date, you're denied access to the software you purchase unless you provide Microsoft with credit card information. No big deal, I thought. I figured there must be an alternative method for confirming your age, to gain access to your Microsoft account, to in turn access your software purchase. What a headache...

So the first thing I did was poke around on the Microsoft website until I stumbled across a Microsoft live chat support link. I don't recall if I found it directly from Google or from Microsoft, but I'm certain it was a Microsoft support representative. I explained that I couldn't log in my account to access my software, which cost me $139.00, because Microsoft was demanding I provide credit card information to verify my age. \\"How could I have purchased the software online with a credit in the first place if I weren't an adult,\\" I asked. I offered to forward the email confirmation from Amazon, purchase order details, and even offered my license number as an alternative method for age verification. The Microsoft support representative ultimately told me they couldn't assist me, and referred me back to Amazon to request a refund. What a waste of time, I thought. I went back to Amazon and explained the issue to not one, not two, but three different Amazon representatives.

In fairness, I'd like to pause here for a moment and say that each Amazon representative made an honest attempt at assisting me with my problem, and I've never had a negative experience with Amazon. Their support is still fantastic in my opinion.

The second Amazon representative with whom I spoke gave me step-by-step instructions on how to get in touch with a Microsoft support representative by phone, but the final step in the instruction guide, 'Click the \\"Request a call button,\\"' brought me right back to the Microsoft login screen. Each time I'd try to login the Microsoft account, however, it would simply demand credit card information again. So in order to reach the support I needed, I had to have access to my newly created Microsoft account, but in order to have access to my account, I needed to speak to support about an alternative method for age verification. It was a frustrating catch-22; a paradoxical situation from which I couldn't escape because of contradictory rules.

Any company (e.g., Microsoft Corp.) that places its bottom line above the convenience and satisfaction of its customers is in general not one I'm particularly comfortable trusting with my credit card information, but it wasn't even a matter of trust so much as a matter of principle. Let's look at it from another perspective: If someone were to purchase something from me, then after the monetary transaction occurred, I demand their credit card information before giving them the item they already paid for, that person would no doubt feel outraged by my lack of ethical competance. Microsoft being a large corporation doesn't change that sentiment one bit.

So I went back to Amazon support, and finally I simply requested a refund for my purchase, since I wasn't able to access the software I purchased. Unfortunately, Amazon explained, because I clicked the URL in the email, the software license was already tied to the account I created at Microsoft, despite the fact that I wasn't able to access it. Thus, they were unable to offer a refund. This was very frustrating but ultimately understandable given the circumstances.

As an alternative, I was given a 1-800 number for direct communication with Microsoft support. I called their support and followed the automated guidance to navigate to the correct department, Accounts and Registration. Upon arriving to the correct department, the automated message instructed me to hang up the phone and access the Accounts department from the website, and it proceeded to hang up on me. By this time I had already spent well over 3 hours trying to troubleshoot this issue. The only thing I wanted was to get in touch with a real Microsoft representative via the phone so I could explain my problem. \\"Surely, they must offer an alternative means for age verification,\\" I thought.

I called Microsoft's 1-800 number again, this time choosing the SALES department, figuring they wouldn't hang up on meagain if they thought they might be in a position to make more money. Fortunately [sad as it may be], my strategy worked and I was able to reach a real live representative. I explained my problem and they in turn explained that there was no way they could assist me in accessing my account over the phone. Despite the fact that I was talking to them in person and they could clearly hear that I wasn't a child, they still demanded credit card information. At one point the representative suggested they might be able to refund my purchase through their \\"money-back guarantee program,\\" but after being placed on hold several times, they returned only to explain that since I couldn't prove the software was defective or not functioning properly, I wasn't eligible for a refund. So alas, I was once again back where I started. It turned out my only options were to snail mail my personal information or provide it to them in the form of credit card information online.

If Microsoft truly had its customer's interests at heart, they would offer an alternative means for age verification. Having been a victim of credit fraud for 8 years during my early adult life, and without the financial means to hire a lawyer to fight it, I've become understandably cautious when it comes to providing my credit card information. I feel like I've been taken advantage of by a company that clearly concerns itself more with its bottom line than the satisfaction and convenience of its paying customers. This coupled with the fact that they apparently don't offer much if any support for customers who've already purchased their software licenses leaves me convinced that despite its reputable history and considerable market influence, it is not a company worthy of the trust it receives. I gave the software 2 stars, because the software itself isn't bad, but it lost 3 stars because dealing with Microsoft has easily been one of the most frustrating and absurdly ridiculous experiences of my life.

Finally, I'll conclude by just stating my intent here is not so much to express my frustration for Microsoft and the recent experience I've had dealing with its [lack of] customer support and effective policies, but rather primarily to give others considering this purchase additional information they might use to make a more informed purchase decision.

Check the listing here to really understand editions, as some users are accidentally purchasing the wrong one. What you are buying here is either a 'Download' stored in your Amazon digital locker complete with license key or a 'Key Card'--plastic card with the license key printed on it that is shipped to you. Both download and key-card involve downloading Office.

Also, Office 2013 is NOT compatible with Windows XP or Vista. It requires you to have Windows 7 or 8.

The Short Form
There were some good ideas behind the improvements to Office 2013, but poor execution, a confusing bid to sell Office 365, and licensing issues (that have since been improved) have tripped up this version of Office. You'll survive with it on a new computer, but there aren't a lot of reasons to upgrade if you already have an existing version of Office.

The Good
If you're a long-time user of Office, there aren't a lot of incentives in Office 2013 to make you want to jump onto the bandwagon apart from the fact that it really does load faster and respond fairly snappily, even on older hardware. The UI is another step beyond what Office 2010 did, offering a flatter-looking ribbon, more stuff dumped into the ribbon, and yet more of those full-screen interface menus that now resemble the 'Modern UI' front-end of Windows 8 and Windows Phone. There are little pleasantries, like files flowing more seamlessly in and out of SkyDrive, and the way the cursor tracks as you type is a surprisingly nice detail. One of the things Microsoft has been trying to do is make your Windows Live/Microsoft/Hotmail/X-Box/SkyDrive account a one-stop shop for all things Microsoft, and so if you set up Windows and/or Office to tie directly into that, little fringe benefits like the aforementioned SkyDrive are dropped into your programs.

Installation of Office 2013 is a breeze--it is surprisingly fast, in minutes if you've already downloaded the files. It's also slightly simpler than earlier versions, getting quickly to the \\"Install now/Customize\\" screen. The first step is a doozy, though: you might start off with an Office 365 prompt that tells you to enter in the e-mail address associated with your Office install. Pay attention to the \\"I want to use a Product Key\\" link on that screen: it flips you from, \\"I'm about to accidentally kick off a 90-day Office 365 Trial\\" to \\"I have a license key, now where do I type it in?\\". The first time I did this I thought this was about tying Office to my Microsoft account, so I went that route and ended up getting e-mails about my Office 365 Trial, how I can use Office via a browser, etc., etc.; and after the trial, I realized my mistake because Office 'deactivated'. I had to go back in and properly 'Activate' office with my key.

The Bad, Lumped In With The Ugly
Unfortunately, we then come to the 'look and feel' and that's where things start to literally get ugly. Office 2013 has a default color palette of \\"One color, black text, and white all over the place.\\" There are two other color schemes, but no other way to customize the interface nor any downloadable themes. All three options, \\"White\\", \\"Light Gray\\", and \\"Dark Gray\\" end up adding to the eyestrain. The menus we lost in the Ribbon of 2007 to 2007's circular candy-button were put back in Office 2010 as colored tabs, and in 2013 they SHOUT AT YOU IN ALL CAPS. \\"FILE HOME VIEW...\\" they say, and I feel like my dad just sent me an e-mail.

My fault for being weird and running two versions, but I tell you this so you know to avoid trying to keep both on the same machine--pick one or the other.

The Bottom Line
If you have a new PC that came with Office 2013 or you work for an organization that makes you move to 2013, there will be times when something you just got used to in 2007 or 2010 has been changed or moved, but you will otherwise get by. Tomorrow I buy the "II" album as MP3. I can upload the Led Zeppelin directory but then it is just up there by itself. If I try to move it to my "Music" directory, I get the following prompt:
"Move Name Conflict. The destination directory already has a file named: ... What do you want to do with the new file? [Skip]" That's right, your only option is to skip. This does not work for me because I do not have particularly fast uploads or a drive big enough to host my entire backup locally.

I can accept the lack of synchronization. In fact I don't actually want that feature because my archives are currently spread across multiple drives and there isn't space on any one device to synchronize a single drive. If you're used to Quicken 2007, you're going to have to get used to a very different interface.

But what sent me back to 2007 is the fact that you can't designate specific lots when selling a security. How can they miss that? You can't correctly calculate capital gain/loss without that! And apparently Intuit doesn't even consider that important enough to mention in their product comparison: http://www.quicken.com/mac/compare
