I've been using Quicken on and off for probably about 20 years. My last Quicken purchase was the 2010 Starter edition--I switched back to Quicken after having abandoned it in favor of GnuCash for a few years. I didn't buy the Deluxe edition because, honestly, the Starter edition does everything I want to do that any version of Quicken is capable of doing--managing my various bank and credit card accounts. I don't really need it to manage loan accounts, and it's incapable of budgeting the way I'd like to, which would be biweekly instead of monthly. C'mon, Intuit--how much longer are you going to ignore those of us who get paid biweekly? (Luckily, the Calendar feature of Quicken provides enough insight into spending that I can use that--I enter all my recurring transactions as reminders, estimating things like groceries and gas and other things I know I'll spend money on, and the calendar shows me how much money is projected to be left in my account on any given day. Good enough.)

So, this morning Quicken 2010 warned me that after April of this year I'd no longer be able to download transactions from my financial institutions unless I upgraded to Quicken 2013. I shouldn't have been surprised--Intuit has been sticking it to its users like this for years, and we continue to put up with it because Quicken is really the only game in town. But just to stick it to us a little more, I couldn't just buy the 2013 Starter edition. Only the Deluxe edition (or higher) would import my existing Quicken data. The Starter edition is only for those who are brand-new to Quicken. So, with gritted teeth I upgraded to Quicken 2013 Deluxe, purchasing the download version here on Amazon.

The software download and subsequent installation went very smoothly. Quicken Deluxe 2013 seamlessly imported my existing data, and when it finally opened for the first time, things looked pretty-much the same as they had in my previous version. That was good enough for me.

Once installed, I explored the application a bit, customizing it for my own needs. I have to say I found little feature-wise that would have compelled me to purchase this upgrade absent the forced obsolescence of my previous version. The one thing I hoped might make it worth the upgrade was the new mobile app and cloud syncing. I created my Quicken Cloud account and synced my accounts, installed the Android app, logged in on my phone, and allowed the Quicken mobile app to sync with my cloud account. Once synced, the opening screen of the mobile app showed me account summary numbers that didn't make any sense to me. I checked my checking account balance and found that it was wildly different than what showed in Quicken on my PC. (I also noticed that both versions showed my online balance to be greatly different than what my bank showed, so that might be related to this problem.) Try as I might, I could never get my mobile app to show balances that were consistent with my PC app. That makes the mobile app completely worthless to me.

[Update on the mobile app: I decided to try one more time with the mobile app. The ending balance it shows for my checking account is still wrong -- it's off by an amount equal to the value of the one transaction that still shows as pending when I view it on my bank's web site. I'd already entered that transaction manually into Quicken Desktop, For some reason the mobile app doesn't know that and is subtracting it from my ending balance (which Quicken Desktop had already done).]

So, no compelling new features in the PC app. A worthless mobile app that shows incorrect information. Quicken 2013 Deluxe gives me absolutely nothing new for the fifty-some bucks I spent, other than the privilege of continuing to be able to download data from my financial institutions. If it weren't for that, I'd still be using my Quicken 2010 Starter edition. The only good thing I can say about Quicken Deluxe 2013 is that it allows me to doeverything I was doing with 2010 Starter. But nothing more.

I was skeptical that a downloadable version of office could really be an excellent program, but I was totally wrong. This is absolutely the best version yet. The one adjustment is to go into the advanced setup and turn off graphics acceleration.If you don't, many of your games will run very slowly. Just uncheck the box and restart any of the programs: it will run even faster without the acceleration, and all your games will hum along as before.

Among the new features, two stand-out: the app store and the spell checker. The app store gives you free access to such programs as The Merriam Webster Dictionary and Legal Zoom Forms. It feels as though you own an iPhone. The add-ins work flawlessly and there are so many that it is absolutely fun to find them. The spell checker in Word solves so many problems that it is worth the money by itself. Not only does it work in the whole document instead of that maddening small window of the past, but it also has a superior ability to find whole words that have accidentally been split by commas or semi-colons. I actually saw it find "did;nt" and offer the correct replacement -- something it was never able to do in the past.

As far as the subscription "tether" - well, if $100 brings all of this, then I welcome it. Every year. Updates come in automatically and smoothly.

One caveat: if you have previously added-in classic menu toolbars in your older versions, disable them. If you haven't, Office 365 will try to use them and then be unable to do so when it starts up. it will search for a way for several minutes before any program, such as Word or Excel, starts. You must go into the setup to add-ins for EACH program and uncheck them (COM add-ins). It is a royal pain. So, disable all those classic menu add-ins before downloading.

Other than that, a superb product, well worth more than the$100 price.

I upgraded from Quicken 2011, so this is a 3-year jump. It was instantly familiar, but there are some worthwhile additions and tweaks. The budgeting is easier to set up and track, as are savings goals and debt reduction. The online updates are improved, they're slightly quicker, and I like the new loan summary screens that show project payoffs and some 'what if' scenarios.

But, this release is sloppy for several reasons. Firstly, the R1 release was done with several known bugs, including one where you can access data after cancelling the password prompt. I reported this on the quicken community website, and was told the bug was fixed in R2 and my thread was locked. I have R2 now, and this bug is not fixed, although others are including serious crashes when accessing older reports. (now fixed, see above)

Another issue is screen refresh. On the registers it's noticeably quicker than older versions (apparently due to using the .NET 4.0 framework), but on screens with graphics (such as the budget screen and loan details screens) the refresh is appallingly slow. I have a very fast PC with dedicated graphics cards, and this makes no difference. This isn't just a slight nuisance, it's practically unusable.

There are other annoyances too, which have been there a while. You still cannot create trend graphs for multiple categories, where the graph shows the breakdown (for example Food, Food: Groceries, Food: Dining out etc). Also, you cannot budget by summary categories, you have to include sub categories and go through a process of moving rollover between categories. Example, if I have Personal Care:Equipment and Personal Care: Activities. I might want to budget $500 for both, but not specify an amount for each. These features have ironically been available on Mint.com (also owned by Intuit) since 2009.

Finally, I understand the mobile side of Quicken 2014 is being updated too, so your old version won't work. This will be released on Oct 1st.

How important these things are to you, may simply be down to how you use the product - but when paying $100+ for a bit of software, which has to be renewed every 3 years, you might expect better. With no viable competition, Intuit really has no incentive to do so. My recommendation; if you're on 2011 or earlier, upgrade. If you're on 2012 or later, it might not be worth it.

I'm torn as to whether to give AIDA 64 Extreme 3 or 4 stars.  Ultimately, based on my intended use and the software's functionality, I go with 3 stars.  Whether I would recommend you purchase this product depends on your desired uses.  I purchased AIDA 64 with the intent to monitor various aspects of my computer (temps, clock speeds, fan speeds, etc.).  I particularly wanted something that had on OSD (on screen display) option.    Pros:  - Copious info on your computer from temps (CPU, CPU package, individual CPU cores, motherboard, GPU, etc.) to memory usage.  If there's info that you want on your computer, you can probably find and/or monitor it with AIDA 64 extreme.  - Fairly good user interface, with one exception (in my opinion).    Cons:  - The OSD cannot be displayed in-game, severely limiting it's usefulness to check temps, etc. when you're gaming.  - The software's use of the sensors conflicts with my Asus software's use of the sensors.  This led to erroneous readings in my Asus software, including an erroneous voltage reading that led to a hard shutdown of my computer due to the Asus anti-surge protection.  I would just get rid of the Asus software, but I use it to control my fans.  AIDA64 doesn't control fans.  - The OSD and desktop displays are buried under \\"file\\" --> \\"preferences\\".  It's odd that they don't get their own drop-down in the main screen like the benchmarking tools do.    The first 2 cons listed seriously limit the usefulness of this software for me. I'll still get some use out of the great depth of info it provides and perhaps will try out the benchmarking/stress test tools.  This software might be more useful for others, such as if they want to use it mostly for the benchmarking tools included (which I haven't explored yet since that wasn't my main focus in purchasing this software), aren't using other software that reads the same sensors, and/or don't care about in-game OSD.

So on the 3rd of May I sat down to check my accounts and Q2012 wouldn't connect to any of the banks I use. A little statement that said we told you in the EUA that connections would be lost 3 years after the purchase so you will be forced into buying a product that you may not want. Not at all happy about that and I don't really know if that is an Amazon or Quicken deal. Either way, be up front about it and don't stick that in a 5 page end user agreement that seems to give you the freedom to do whatever. As another reviewer said, Quicken is about the only game in town. I'm sure there are others but it's like Windows was (the most used, most popular piece of stuff out on the market). Downloaded the product and installed it. That part was easy; then it went through its install questions as if you had never been a Q user before. So starting from that point I was not happy but it finally asked if I was an Intuit "member" and allowed me to use my previous ID and password to get started. Next it wanted to know if I wanted to use my old password for my password vault to keep prying eyes off of the accounts... turns out this is just a way to keep the files locked until you want to actually see them before you update them (I'll have to find a way to turn that off). Next it converts your old 2012 files into a new file and you get to start all over with your bank accounts and restarting the web express or direct download. Surprisingly, once you go to TOOLS-> ACCOUNT LIST and get your account to edit, it highlights your bank name so you think you can hit next and reestablish connections. NOPE. You have to retype your bank name and then hit NEXT. And of course it finds your accounts under your username and password but it doesn't initially allow you to link the new files with the old accounts (my checking, my savings, my whatever) so I end up with my old accounts and 3 duplicates with only a 60 day history. I had to go back and start again but this time it allowed me to link the accounts so my accounts are all in place with all of my history from 1995. Next step was to delete the duplicates. At least that went OK. After the first account was set up, I tried the other accounts (after converting each file) and used just the "one step update" tool. That worked a lot better. Pretty seamless, actually. I was able to link accounts to the old named files and all went well. Then everything synched to the cloud (I thought I might use the IPad app since the two are supposed to work together). I installed the app on the IPad and found I could only see one account. That bites! and the app doesn't give you account details, only a summary. Apparently, Intuit wants you use the one step update tool only because it has taken the account actions drop down menu away (on the top right hand side of each account)  and replaced it with a little gear icon. You have to do some exploring here and I think the "named" drop down menu is better than the gear (this is a desktop version, not a smart phone version). Aside from those quirks and irritations, it appears to work basically the same. When I have a free day, I'll go into it a little deeper and see if Q changed investments or tax tools or the what if scenarios.

I use Outlook at work and have no choice about that.  I have used Thunderbird at home for many years but since Mozilla stopped supporting it, I have had a number of problems with Thunderbird.  I looked around and decided that the only viable alternative, for my use, would be Outlook.  I receive 50 to 80 emails a day and send probably 20 or 30.  I keep 1.5 to 2 years worth of emails for historical purposes so I am a heavy email user.  I read the reviews of Outlook 2013 here, many of which are quite negative.  I gritted my teeth and plowed forward.  First of all, the download was half the estimated size.  The installer was less than 1mb and the product was around 500mb, not 1gb as listed.  Also, I have a broadband connection but the download time was under 20 minutes.  Not bad at all.  I did have to open an account at Microsoft and that took a while.  The only part of that that upset me was that they sent me an email to verify the account and email was what I did NOT want to use because of the problems with Thunderbird.  I solved that by using webmail and responding to the Microsoft email online; it worked.  The download and install went well and didn't take particularly long.  I am running Windows 7 Home Premium.  The process of setting up multiple email accounts took a little time but was quite smooth.  I had to supply very little information; Outlook figured out most of it by itself.  Once installed, I had to look around to find it because the install didn't put an icon on the desktop.  I like to have my software on the desktop and for email I like to pin the icon to the task bar so I don't have to go hunting to start it.  Once it started, it worked fine.  The interface is very close to the Outlook 2010 interface that I use at work so there was no learning curve there.  Overall I am quite pleased, so far.  The reason I gave the product 4 stars instead of 5 primarily is because Microsoft dropped support of the ALT key functions that I have been using for the past 30plus years on PCs.  Microsoft has never been very good about backward compatibility and this product is no exception.  I use the ALT key functions (Alt E, C for copy; Alt E P for paste, Alt F S for save, Alt F X for exit, etc.) all the time because they are quicker and more convenient than using a mouse or trackball for the same purpose.  Other than that I really have no complaints at all about Outlook 2013.  And there are a couple of things I like about it:  The default setup is with the accounts/folders shown on the left, a list of emails in the inbox in the center and a display of the current email on the right; that's pretty convenient.  Thunderbird has a similar capability but the list and the display are vertically oriented and don't work as well for me as the Outlook setup.  The other thing I like about Outlook, is the up and down arrows allowing you to jump from one email to the next; it is more convenient than anything I found with Thunderbird.  Would I recommend the product to anyone else?  With qualifications, yes, I would.

In order to use bitlocker, your computer must have a TPM chip in it.  If not, you can turn bitlocker on but have to use a USB drive to hold the key file every time you boot it up.  An acceptable solution for a desktop, but for a laptop a bit of an inconvenience having a USB drive sticking out of it, plus it takes up a USB port.  My 2 month old Dell XPS laptop had the option of having Win 7 Home Premium, Professional, or Ultimate installed, so I assumed I could upgrade afterwards.  Turns out they must only put that chip into models shipping with Ultimate already.  So double check that if bitlocker is important to you.    Other than this issue, the update process was quick and painless.  It seemed to take less time than installing a regular software program since it didn't have to load off the CD and do a lot of registry changing.    Ultimate itself with the XP mode seems a good upgrade for me.  A few hardware items and some software just doesn't work with Win 7.  Plus I needed encryption for some files.  While I use some third party encryption, it's just easier for some files if the OS does it without having to log into another software.  Some of the other differences between Ultimate and Professional aren't relevant to me, so Professional was probably a better match.    3/28/11 Additional note: Found a website that says the TPM chip not only handles the encryption key, it actually does the encrypting and decrypting activity so that the CPU does not have to.  When using a USB drive for the key, the CPU does the encrypting/decrypting which reduces performance.

Rather than reading the data file from those programs, TaxAct reads the PDF output files. Unfortunately, while it imports the basic stuff like name,address, and capital gain/loss carryovers, it completely ignores much important information that you would expect it to import, like Schedule B payers, depreciated items, IRA basis, etc. Review your previous year's return carefully and make sure that all relevant values are transferred!  Another area that could definitely use improvement is the integration between the state and federal returns. Although around since 2008, TaxAct still seems a bit immature in its interface. I found the following issues, which Ireported to TaxAct, to be an annoyance but fortunately not a showstopper:  1. A warning should be provided when overwriting the value of an item detail sum.  2. Once an item detail sum is overwritten, deleting the entered value in some cases simply sets the value to 0, while in other cases produces a dialog explaining that the detail sum value will be restored. In the case of the former, the sum value cannot be restored in any obvious way. It is necessary to edit the detail to change its sum and save it, then to go back and restore the detail to the desired value and save it again.  3. 1099-R: If a numeric code is accidentally selected in box 7, then even after selecting an alpha code there is no way to remove the numeric code.  4. California state tax return: Poor integration with Federal return – the Open Supporting Form feature is not available on most/all values on the state return, e.g. Form 540 line 13.  8. The escape key should be allowed to close an item detail popup if the value has not been modified.  9. Override rules and text color are inconsistent and confusing. Some values, e.g. Estimated Tax Worksheet line 2, display as green (indicating a user-entered value), and yet the program populates that value if the user does not provide an entry. Once the user does so, there is no indication if it is a calculated (auto-updating) entry or a user-provided entry. I would like to see such values designate something like "weak-overrides" which are calculated values which may be typed over and which require a confirmation when the user does so. They should not prevent e-filing as do  "hard-override" values, and are flagged during the review only if the user requests to see those values. They should be indicated by a yellow background with either blue or green text, depending on if the value has been auto-calculated or manually entered.  10. I have observed that selecting a different file directory makes the program crash (not repeatable). After the program crashed, it failed to successfully transmit an error report.  11. Securities Traders report income on Form 6781 which correctly flows to Schedule D.  That income however fails to flow to 4562 line 11. Overriding that value (or any other) prevents the return from being E-filed.  12. Save as PDF: The file has no index.  13. A strange mix of highly powerful tools that provide precise control and default dimensions that are locked in so you can't actual modeling an existing structure. Unfortunately, the interface is so complicated that it's hard to figure out if a needed capability is there, or has been crippled to entice you to upgrade to the \\"Pro\\" version.
For example, when you build a wall, you can not only control it's width, you get four (or more) options for the interior components of the wall. But a floor is a floor, and the height is permanently set at 12 5/8\\". If you're floor is less than that, you're model will be too tall, forcing other dimensions out of whack. Hardly something only a \\"Pro\\" would want.
Be careful of the \\"Product Compare\\" on their website - it indicates this version has the \\"Best\\" tools for Remodeling, equivalent to Pro. It doesn't.
The interface could use some improvement, especially as it's not supposed to be geared at professional users. For example, setting a garage floor height to ground level requires an understanding of Stem Wall Tops, and even then seems to override any attempt to let you actually put it at ground level. There are not hotkeys for most functions, including common ones such as view panning and using most dimension tools. 3D view navigation can be clumsy and buggy.
Automatic tools such as stairwell creation and roof generation are not impressive, doing things like causing significant cosmetic errors, or disappearing an entire floor. But at least in some cases, you can override the with manual settings.
That all being said, much of the feature set is outstanding. For example, a good selection of built-in items (door styles, fixtures, etc.) and precision control over things like stair geometry. Just too bad some important elements are crippled.

As a new user, I found Quicken 2013 difficult to get fully up and running. Specifically, it was difficult to add enough past transaction history into Quicken to perform reasonable analyses (two years in my case). The connection to my bank and download of accounts was a snap, but since Wells Fargo only provided the last 90 days of transactions and VISA only the last 60 days, I spent the next week trying to learn how to import the rest. After several failed attempts, exhaustive internet searches for help, and after purchasing several converters from ProperSoft, I finally got everything to work.

Recommendations to new users: don't use the automatic setup feature. Instead: (1) choose the date range you want* and download QFX files from your bank to your computer, (2) import the files into Quicken using Web Connect (not Express Web Connect) - this prevents connection to your bank during import, (3) make sure the imports look good, (4) go to Tools/Account-List, and for each account click Edit, go to the Online Services tab, and change the connection method to Express Web Connect or Direct Connect as desired. At this point you are ready for your first automatic update with your bank. Do the update and check the accounts (you will probably need to change your \\"Opening Balance\\" to get the right current balance).

* Note that to be able to import QFX files using Web Connect, my bank (and Quicken) required that the desired start date and balance correspond to the start date and balance on a past monthly statement.

Adding sufficient Credit Account history is similar but a little harder. Your bank may not even let you download more than 60 days directly, so you will first need to manually cut and paste data from old statements into a spreadsheet, format the data for CSV to QIF conversion, buy a converter (ProperSoft CSV2QIF converter works well), convert the data, and import the QIF file into Quicken.

Recommendations to Quicken (and associated financial institutions): (1) provide at least two years of transaction history for Quicken automatic set up (this includes VISA and the like), (2) if you can't do recommendation 1, then add more comprehensive set up instructions and add capability for Quicken to import csv files (or provide converters with new orders).

This review concerns only the download and installation experience for this product, Rosetta Stone Dutch, level 1, for Mac. As I use the product I might update this review.  As a Mac user, I'm accustomed to buying software on the App Store. Download and installation is automatic and fast. The download/install process for this product is as far from that experience as one could imagine. It's stunningly terrible, and I am not being hyperbolic.  First you need to download, mount, and launch Amazon's proprietary download software. What? In 2015?  Then, using Amazon's software, you download the product, which arrives in a disk image. You run the installer from the disk image, supplying your admin credentials.  Then you launch the software you bought, and rather than starting to use it, you are required to start updating. For me, I had to go through a sequence of two updates, each of which required download (each well over 100 MB), admin password entry, and acceptance of terms and conditions.  So, about 45 minutes in to this process (that's if you're lucky enough to have very fast broadband to accommodate the four downloads you've performed), you again try launching the product you bought. This time it does not prompt for yet another update. Yay? No. It asks you to insert your CD-ROM disk.  Of course, as a download product, there is no CD-ROM disk.  After trying various approaches to get around this problem, which included searching first on Amazon for help and then on the Rosetta Stone support pages for help, I was, one could say, well surprised but not delighted.  I then found, buried deep behind a labyrinth of unhelpful content on the Rosetta Stone site, a link to initiate a live chat session. Which I did. If the single star I've awarded indicates anything positive, it's that they do offer chat support, and it's available apparently any time of day.  The person who helped me was indeed able to help me solve the problem, but only because I could second guess his poor instructions. For example, he wrote "click" the the chat window when he meant "double click," and he asked me to move a file from a mounted disk image to the Desktop when that step is entirely unnecessary. In our chat, he wrote wonderfully ambiguous instructions such as "Please drag the file."  It turned out that to use the software I purchased, I had to use Finder to navigate to a hidden folder, create a new folder within it, name that folder with a particular case-sensitive name, and then drag a 400 MB file from the mounted, original disk image, into the folder I had manually created and named.  Then I could use the software.  Then I had to get past the mandatory registration process (of course, at this point I invented a name, email address, age, and so on, because the company had long since burned any remnant of trustworthiness). But I still couldn't use the program I'd purchased.  The running app then opened my web browser and sent me to an associated website, which prompted me, rather rudely, to install Adobe Flash. No. I just closed that Safari window, and then, back in the app, deselected the checkbox that had been selected by default to always send me to the web.  I wanted to learn a bit of Dutch. Instead I learned that this product, which is just level one of a multilevel sequence and which nominally costs more than a hundred dollars, has a 1995 style installation experience, and a horrible one even given that framing.  Wow.

I'm a convert from MS Money, which was a free application offered with a laptop purchase long ago.  I was never satisfied with MS Money and as a consequence I managed most of my budgeting and bookkeeping via spreadsheets.    Because I could never easily leverage my bank's ability to download transaction history (combined with my strict use of debit cards for 99% of purchases), spreadsheets were hard to manage and I frequently fell out of the habit of using them.    I hadn't tried Quicken in the past because of a rather disappointing experience with  Quickbooks.  However, that was nearly a decade ago and I was really desperate for a better way to budget and track against it.  To my pleasant surprise, Quicken has done the job quite well.    Overall, it's much easier to use than MS Money ever was and the built-in data feeds from my banks was a great help.  Rather than pulling a file off the bank's website and then uploading into Quicken (followed by the always-painful manual sync and reconciliation process), Quicken handles all of the work behind the scenes.    There -is- a learning curve to the product, but it's no more severe than any other average application I've used.  One nice touch for anyone less inclined towards tweaking is the way that Quicken handles assignment of expense/income category assignment and payee memorization.  When you change the name of a payee in a register entry, Quicken will create rules to re-name that payee in the future.  If you'd like to manually edit the rules yourself, you can.  In fact, you can go just about as far down into the detail of this process as you like, or alternatively, not at all, without sacrificing any other functionality.    On the downside, the product could offer more guidance and provide more notifications on what it is automatically handling, especially when creating a budget.  The process is very simple, but unlike tracking expenses and income, creating recurring payments and deposits is a bit of a challenge.  Quicken handles most of it for you, but if you want to customize, it seems like you'll need to provide a lot more detail than you may expect (especially in cases when you're setting up a paycheck, where Quicken would like you to use your last check stub to create the recurring event).    However, that functionality isn't a required element for a successful implementation of a budget. If you’re after a simple GPS or mapping program, others are freely available. And this program is about as far from “simple” as any software I’ve ever written, reviewed, tested, or even seen. It’s “EZ Nav Route Wizard” is their sad attempt at providing a simpler interface by bypassing most of their "features", but it’s power is nil. If you want simple directions from one place to another, that’s their way of giving it to you. However, I’m baffled by why, if that’s what you’re after, you’re even considering this. What DeLorme should have done, instead of wasting time developing a goofy simplistic option like this and sticking it in their ridiculously bulky and inefficient program is spend some time and effort simplifying the entire thing. Imagine the control panel/dashboard of a 777 jetliner, with a seemingly infinite array of stuff, and a button in the middle that says “Fly to Chicago”. Yeah, nice idea DeLorme. Why not just make the thing easier to fly? See, the bottom line is none of us is trying to fly a jetliner, we’re just trying to drive to a few places as quickly, easily and efficiently as possible, and we don’t need the dash of a 777 to do it.

If, like many people who were abandoned by Microsoft when they stopped producing Streets & Trips even though it was consistently rated #1, you’re looking for a program that serves as a GPS and a routing program, DELORME STREET ATLAS IS NOT IT. This program has extremely limited power in this regard – so much so that there’s no way to include it in that category. If you, for instance, have a round trip to plan, where you know your start and end points, and have multiple stops to make but aren’t sure what order to put them in, or lets say you’re a service technician or salesman or a delivery person and you’re trying to maximize your efficiency by adjusting your start and stop times for each day, along with the duration of each of your stops, throwing sticks to the wind and trying to make sense of where they land might be more productive than using DeLorme SA. It allows for NO start or stop time, and entering a duration for each stop is enough to make you want to hurt people. As a comparison, in MS S&T, if you want to adjust your start time or a stop’s duration, you simply double click that address in the left pane, which lies in the same window as the place where you entered it. Up pops the time window for that stop. If you want to do it in DeLorme SA, here are the steps… make sure you’re in the Route tab. Then click the Advanced button on the bottom left. Then locate (scroll if necessary) the stop you’d like to adjust and click on it in the center pane. Then click the Stop Pref’s button on the right side. NOW you can enter a duration for your stop. It makes me imagine a microwave where the some of the number buttons are on the left of the microwave, some are in the middle below the door, and the rest of the buttons are on the right side, and they seem to have forgotten to put a "start" button on the thing. And for good measure, let’s remove all the quick setting buttons from the microwave. You know, the quick minute button and all those – they’re way too useful.

My bottom line for this software is you’re probably only looking at it for one of a few reasons, and it just doesn’t do a good job at ANY of them. You’re options for a Streets and Trips replacement are thin for sure, and I’m still looking. If that’s what you’re in search of, good luck, SA is NOT IT. If you need a simple GPS/mapping program, this is NOT IT. Simple isn’t apparently in this software team’s vocabulary. And if you’re looking for a routing program of any kind, with any level of efficiency to it atall, this is also NOT IT.

This functionality was available in a previous version, but was removed and never brought back.

For example, I have two accounts that I clicked on \\"Do not show this screen again\\" for the \\"Reconciliation Complete\\" screen, but I cannot get this screen back when doing the reset. The first use of the new software and some of the features were a bit wobbly, i.e., the drop down lists in Billminder (weeks/months/Account List) were blank. A reboot and fresh open of the software solved that. I hooked accounts up with Quicken Mobile, an obvious mirror to the Mint app that Intuit purchased and quite frankly, that app has worked across a Droid phone, and a Samsung Galaxy Tablet without problems. I think I had one handshake account refresh that failed, but I believe it was a wireless signal issue on my end. I almost gave this 5 stars (again, I've used the heck out of Quicken for decades so I'm pretty versed in the nuances) but I really wanted to give the online connections a couple of weeks to see if I experience any of the issues that some of the reviewers have reported. At this point I would say 2014 is connecting and downloading from my financial institutions better than 2011 was in the end. After many calls and lots of digging on the internet, I just discovered why the Norton Anti-SPAM doesn't do anything. My problem has been that while I mark e-mails as SPAM, and they go into the blocked list, but the next SPAM mail comes into my in-box and sits there.

Based on what I see on Google, this is a common problem. It turns out that Norton only can watch the two (antique) e-mail ports that hardly any e-mail service now uses. Those are 110 and 25. When you try ot add the right ports, it claims those are used by other applications (which is nonsense). None of the three services I routinely use support those any more. Norton claims that hey can't watch the SSL/TLS ports now used, because they can't see encrypted content. That's ridiculous for several reasons. Once in my in-box, the e-mails are not encrypted...so much for "Outlook integration". It also means that if I use the secure ports my providers insist on, then I can't use Norton Anti-SPAM...the whole reason I bought Norton 360 in the first place.

So, it's now gone from my systems.

I work at a church, and we have avast! Free as our antivirus. I use Ad-Aware on my own computer, so that's what I use for general comparison.

PROS:

avast! does what it says it does. It doesn't score the highest in the antivirus tests that individual organizations put out, but it still scores generally pretty high for a free version. It has prevented some gunk getting into my computer at work, sometimes multiple times in quick succession.

I turned off the web app a while back because it was slowing down IE. I've updated to IE11 (still slows down opening windows, tabs, and pages by .29s) and now use Chrome for Drive, but I don't know how the add-on acts with Chrome since I left it turned off there as well. If I remember correctly, the add-on offered a number of features such as shopping deals that seemed to beat items you were viewing (same item, different site/posting) and blocking ad tracking. I could be confusing Ad-Aware and avast!...

avast! monitors your main programs and makes sure you know when they're outdated, such as Adobe Reader, Adobe Air, web browsers, and java. It will even check the installation files of popular programs and prompt you to download the latest version if it happens to be outdated, thus saving you some update time later. It also gives an internal option for updating so you don't have to search all over and do the updates individually. Of course, you have to make sure to check the "I don't agree" box when you do update through avast!, otherwise you will end up with extra programs installed. Just be smart and that feature will be worth it.

You can track your devices secured with avast! through the interface by signing in, so there is no going to their site through your browser to check on that. It's good to have the quick reference right there with everything else.

The interface is well-designed, simple to use, and aesthetically pleasing. The simple part is important.Some antivirus interfaces can be confusing, as Ad-Aware's interface is not quite as user-friendly.

CONS:

I'm ok with them offering extra features very now and then, but one of the computers here has pop-ups in the corner (not very big, but noticeable) just about every time we use it (3-4x/week). The upside is that the pop-ups looks good enough that they are not visually irritating. I just wish I could turn them off since we won't be adding them anytime soon.

SUMMARY:

If you are wanting an antivirus that is easy to use and generally well-rated, this antivirus will do for you. It stays in the market as a recommended antivirus, and it really does work well, in my experience.

At least Intuit is consistent. That is, consistent in undershooting the mark. Why, why, why, for example, does Intuit insist on forcing the Brokerage structure on users. The problem with the Brokerage structure is that every active investment from a particular institution is conflated into a single account. These account entries are hard enough to read as it is. It's the equivalent of giving the user data reports only after the reports have been processed through a shredder and then through a shake-and-bake baggie.

Another downside to this choice is that if you have several accounts at one institution, you can only download into one of those accounts. Then, of course, you have to go through and delete data from all the other accounts to clean up the one account, AND THEN you have the pleasurable task of manually keying in the data for all the other accounts.

And what's the deal with "Market Value"? Seems it should be a fairly straight-forward math problem: # of shares x current market price. That formula works only if you don't make "Dividend Income" entries with your "Reinvest Dividend" entries. How is a user supposed to make use of the "Dividend Income" report if there is no dividend income entered?

And, same as previous incarnations, the support for Quicken for Mac is close to abysmal AGAIN. The whole point of the Mac system is to make the user experience as intuitive as possible. Trying to figure how to make effective use of the Investments component of Quicken is brutal, time-consuming, and most definitely NOT intuitive.

On the bright side, including the Investments module in Quicken 2015 for Mac fixes the most glaring inadequacy of Quicken Essentials. It seems to me that Intuit just does not really want to support the Mac product. They'd much rather devote their energies to reaping huge profits from making loans. I can see how they might think that anyone who can effectively manage money, using their software or not, would be least likely to become a debtor. If you need an on-line \\"check register,\\" this is about as simple and efficient as you can get, short of creating and maintaing your own Excel spreadsheet. Nobody actually uses checks any more (do they?) but you still need to track payments and deposits when you pay your bills online. You enter transactions into Quicken and watch your balance change accordingly. Recurring payments (like the mortgage) can be programmed to appear in the register automatically every month.

End of month reconciliation with the bank is a breeze (which it would not be in Excel). You can switch easily between multiple bank accounts. At end of year, or at tax time, it's easy to create a report by expenditure category to see how much you spent on utilities, health care, charity, credit cards, or any other payee. If your bank is Quicken-compatible, your online bill payments can be automatically downloaded into your Quicken register.

On the down side, the software is replete with mega-bloat. The company wants to own your entire financial world, including investments, savings, mortage, loans, insurance and 401(k) accounts. If you don't mind having all your eggs in one basket, that could be a good thing. Personally, I wouldn't trust any one company with all that information.

All I need is an expense and income register, so I downloaded the simplest and cheapest of their many products. I don't want Quicken's tentacles attached to my bank accounts so I enter online banking transactions manually into the software, which amounts to double entry. Call me crazy, but I'm very protective of my hard-earned money.

Also, the Quicken categories by which you organize your expenditures are bizarre, redundant, and hard to control. I have one called Household: Utilities: Utilities:Utilities. Seriously. I haven't yet figured out how to dial back that exuberance.

There are free check register apps out there, but none work as smoothly as this one. If online banking software would ever get their act together and show real functional balances instead of building in the 3 to 10 day lag in payments processing and deposits clearing, then a lot of the need for separate software like Quicken would evaporate. Until that day, you need a register like Quicken to monitor your real-time bank balance. If you want to merge your many bank accounts (big bank, credit union, brokerage account, loan shark, etc.) into one place, then Quicken is also a good choice.

The feature in the new Quicken 2014 mobile app that allows you to snap and store receipts is awesome. You have to buy the Quicken 2014 desktop program to use the Quicken 2014 mobile app. You snap a picture of your receipt with your mobile phone and it will attach itself to the associated spending entry on the Quicken mobile app.

When you sync the mobile data to the desktop data, the receipt's picture is automatically attached to the correct spending entry on the desktop program and stored in the Quicken Cloud, which can then be downloaded to your desktop. I like to use the [[ASIN:B0070J9GOU Xerox Mobile Wi-fi Scanner]] with my iPhone to get a really good pic of the receipt. That works in the Quicken 2014 app as well, since it will allow you to attach any picture stored on your phone to your spending entry. It's a very efficient way to keep track of your receipts, especially for business expenditures.

This is a lot better than the [[ASIN:B001CQFRPO NeatReceipts Mobile Scanner and Digital Filing System - PC]] system since it is all on one app. The Neat Receipts system requires a lot of steps and a lot of time to attach a picture of a receipt to your spending entry in Quicken. Their mobile photo system is similar to the Quicken system in that it puts the receipt in the Neat cloud, but it also requires a rather expensive monthly subscription.

My only hesitation about Quicken 2014 is that there are very few other new features in the upgrade, so if the receipt picture feature is not important, then I'm not sure it would be worth the upgrade price, especially if you are upgrading from Quicken 2013.

I work with many high-end software programs, such as Steinberg Cubase and Adobe Photoshop, and I can say without a doubt that MS Street & Trips is the most needlessly counter-intuitive software program I've ever used. It's not hard to use -- rather it just doesn't function the way anyone would want or expect a GPS software program to function. If you use it every day, you can get used to the backwards interface, but for someone like me who uses the software every now and then, it's so frustrating it would drive a person mad.

The details:

I want to point out right away that I don't use GPS for planning long trips with rest stops, calculating mileage, points of interest, etc. My only purpose for MS Streets & Trips is to simply know where I am at all times, and to occasionally plan routes to gigs and back since I am a weekend warrior musician. Once you tell the software to start tracking, it does a great job of it. (I use a GlobalSat BU-353 receiver.) You always know where you are. The additional map configurations (political, terrain, and especially nighttime) are very handy, the speedometer is dead-on accurate, and installation onto my ASUS tablet running Win 7 Pro was a breeze.

But that's pretty much where the accolades end.

The automatic route planner has major issues. It can choose some pretty weird paths. If the software chooses a funky route and you want to change it, you can't fix it just by moving or dragging it. (Why, that would make too much sense!) Instead, you have to set up \\"stops\\" so that the software follows along the path of the stops. Editing your route this way is a pain in the butt, because the software can be stubborn and want to send you on unnecessary 'round-the-block goose chases. (And to set up stops, you have to exit the mode that you had to enable for the software to plan a route in the first place. What???) So, anytime you use this program to create a route, even though it will get you from A to B, plan on spending time going over the entire route and manually inserting stops to correct all of the route's \\"mistakes\\". Otherwise you'll be listening to an incessant, mechanical voice blaring \\"Off route!\\".

The maps themselves are not great, but they're acceptable. There's no font smoothing to speak of, which is sorely needed, but at least you can enlarge the text for easier reading. Microsoft seems to have adopted Google's senseless \\"white streets on an off-white background\\" color scheme, but the product offers optional maps: terrain, political, and nighttime map. In my opinion, the terrain map is perfect for daytime driving, and the nighttime map is great for night driving.

The construction update information seems useless. MS Streets and Trips kept insisting on connecting me to the freeway via a ramp that had been closed for construction for almost a year.

But it's the counter-intuitiveness of this software that is most annoying. For example, I entered a destination and wanted the software to tell me how to get there, but the \\"Plan Route\\" button was disabled. I had to exit the route planning sidebar and call up another sidebar which had a button for creating a route from my current location, or \\"press F3\\". And when the route was created, I was unable to move the map around to preview the route it gave me! And when I wanted to fix the routes mistakes by setting up stops, I had to exit the mode the software used to plan the route in the first place. Arrrrgh! This is one annoying program!

In summary, this program does a great job of tracking your whereabouts, and it's loaded with features. The map quality could be improved, but it's acceptable. I was a long-time Microsoft Money user, and a reluctant Quicken 2011 Premier user since late 2010 (once Microsoft announced it was no longer updating Money). The transition was somewhat laborious and annoying, but I have since grown used to Quicken. Yes, it has its quirks, but I have never lost any data and I have grown more and more dependent on it and more familiar with it over time.

Based on scathing reviews of 2012 and 2013 versions, I never tried to upgrade to those versions and have no experience with them. The reviews of previous versions are similar to other reviews for 2014 in that most claim very few (positive) changes hence no real reason to upgrade. Alas, soon my online updates in Quicken 2011 will stop working in April 2014 due to Quicken's policy of only supporting the last 3 versions (2014, 2013, 2012). At least they are consistent - this has been their policy for 10+ years. I love automatic updates of my accounts, so I bit the bullet and purchased Quicken 2014 Premier.

I think a lot of people are in my shoes... Waiting as long as you can (3 years) before being forced to upgrade from 2011 to 2014 due to the syncing capability expiring, and begrudgingly upgrading and wondering if it will make your life better or worse. So this review is written from that perspective... 2011 vs 2014.

First of all, the upgrade process was fairly straight-forward. I didn't lose any data, there were no errors, and all customized reports came across just fine.

I don't get too worked up over cosmetic or even functional changes but instead put the effort into learning the new application and generally am OK with whatever changes the vendor makes in the long run. In this case there REALLY isn't anything to worry about - Quicken 2014 looks almost identical to 2011. There are a few minor changes such as color scheme. More accounts show up in the account bar (new \\"Separate\\" group for accounts that don't show up under \\"Banking\\", \\"Investing\\", etc. groups). Some dialog/input boxes look different but offer the same functionality. One annoyance is that the pencil/blue dot in the register to indicate Manually Entered / Reviewed downloaded transaction sometimes gets covered up by a new balloon tooltip that prevents you from getting the context menu that allows you to mark it as Reviewed. But overall, it looks very similar.

The One Step Update process is a bit different - one less dialog to click through (especially if you are using password vault) - so that is good, but it does look different. I can't tell that it is any faster at updating accounts than 2011, however. I have been having problems updating my PayPal account in Q2011, and in Q2014 it still had problems but generated a lot more error dialogs that kept getting in my way, so I ended up disabling syncing of my PayPal account altogether.

There is now a way to close accounts instead of only hiding them. This helps in reducing the number of accounts to choose from in account droplists, for example.

I also like the ability to see upcoming scheduled entries in the register - very nice enhancement, although I haven't worked with this too much yet.

The mobile app... I have an Android phone, and it is nice to see recent transactions and such, but really nothing too exciting here. My wife has an iPad and I have to say the iPad app is actually pretty nice - I was pleasantly surprised - very smooth and fluid and modern. The main way we use it is to keep track of our monthly budget/spending progress. Our original (default) budget had way too much detail & too many categories in it, so we created a new and separate \\"Discretionary\\" budget that had limited categories (dining out, gas, etc but not fixed things like mortgage) to make it easier to view on the iPad. It is nice that you can determine which one (and only one) budget to sync to mobile devices. This is nice since Quicken is on my laptop and I travel quite a bit, so it is easy for my wife to keep up-to-date on everything while I am away.

Many times when syncing, Quicken will hang and/or crash. I can't seem to spot a consistent condition that causes this to happen. Again, I haven't lost any data, but this behavior doesn't instill confidence, either. At one point I was running into enough crashes that I ended up disabling mobile sync (Quicken Cloud syncing) altogether to essentially reset everything, then re-enabled mobile Quicken Cloud syncing. Since then, it has been a bit more stable, but not perfect. The initial sync takes a LONG time... be prepared to wait 10-15 minutes even on a high speed connection (100Mbit up/down office connection), but the incremental sync after that is reasonable (less than 30 seconds). I am syncing 17 accounts and the small \\"discretionary\\" budget.

Overall, I'm not mad that I upgraded, but not ecstatic either. I wish it were more stable and efficient and that there were a real competitor out there to keep Intuit on their toes. Overall it has been an OK experience.

I don't know if that is a problem that Quicken can solve or not since it seems to have more to do with how the bank operates.

Overall, this is a step in the right direction. It isn't perfect and I waffled between giving the product 3 or 4 stars. I went with 3 because it appears to be heading in the right direction, but needs some work.

I was very hesitant to make this upgrade from 2010, after reading the long list of negative reviews, but so far I'm okay with this purchase. I have been a Quicken user since the 1990s. This version looks and feels and works like Quicken always has, and I've always been basically happy with the software. I had no problems with upgrading or initial synchronization, unlike some other customers have noted. Aside from seeing some differences between versions, it was a transparent, fast and painless upgrade process.

I give this program 3 instead of 5 stars solely because of the three-year expiration in online services. New customers really need to understand this before they get involved with Quicken. Financial software is something of a long-term relationship, and this becomes a significant cost factor in making your selection. I depend on the online features for tracking a large number of bank balances and online services. I understand WHY they require the periodic refresh (online service formats change over time) but it's still highly frustrating to be FORCED to upgrade. Changing versions is annoying at best, and difficult at worst, and it comes with a real monetary cost. If they wanted to, Intuit COULD design Quicken so that those features alone could be updated separately. Obviously, forcing a comprehensive upgrade (without offering a true upgrade price) is part of their business model, and they deserve to be dinged for that alone. Fortunately, the excellent Amazon price (>60% off the Intuit asking price) makes it easier to swallow this year.

Some changes I noticed right away, compared to Q2010:
- The online tools have fixed some visual refresh issues when the post-update summary was shown. Nice.
- The synchronization/download process is MUCH faster now. Nice.
- The cleared/reconciled marker now shows a popup selection tool. Takes LONGER to change multiple items. Not nice.
- Some minor interface look-and-feel differences.Meh.
- The software self-updated upon initial installation. Nice.
- My Q2010 files were quickly loaded and updated (yes, I backed them up before trusting this new version). Nice.
- Register transactions have a handy set of action buttons at the right. Nice.
- I spotted a few new options that will allow me to prevent certain things that really bugged me in Q2010, like certain autofill and autocorrect actions. Nice.

I refuse to touch the mobile tools; first, there are still too many negative reviews, and second, I am unwilling to upload sensitive financial information and account numbers into the cloud. My 2013 Deluxe version is an upgrade from my "old" Quicken 2010 version. With my dismay, the 2013 version maintains the same flaws that were affecting the older version. Specifically, the program disregards any transaction posted or recorded after today's date. An example: I buy something for $10 with my ATM card on 2/10 and run the transaction as a credit card (i.e. not a pin transaction). I go home and record that transaction before it gets posted in my bank account. Since I do not know exactly when that transaction will be posted in my bank account, I record that $10 transaction as of 2/12. On 2/11 that transaction is posted in my bank account and I update my bank account online on that day. Well, even though I had previously registered that exact transaction as of 2/12, Quicken does not "see" the exact match in the register and flags that transaction as "new". Moreover, if I manually match that transaction with my previous entry, Quicken does not update the actual posting or clearing date and leaves the date unchanged. In the example 2/12. As a result, the posting date in my bank account (2/11) and the posting date in my Quicken register (2/12) do not match. By comparison, my old Microsoft Money program saw all the post dated transactions in the register, automatically matched them and updated the posting date according to the bank records. Is it too much for Quicken to do?

After contacting Quicken Technical Support, I was asked to the send them the log files from my Quicken so they can solve my issue. The program automatically checks for state and federal updates throughout tax season, and updating takes but a mouse click. Several years ago TurboTax was messing with people's hard disk sectors and that did not sit well withme. I have tried the H&R Block program, but their direct-form-entry interface is horrible. This is the worst version of Quicken I have used yet. I only bought it because I was nearing the end of support for downloads in Quicken 2011, and Intuit basically forces you to upgrade every 3 years. The first impression of this version was horrible. Once it installed (which took absurdly long), it couldn't read my existing data file; I had to use Intuit's password-removal tool to remove the password from the file. This requires uploading your file to Intuit, then downloading it again, which is a huge pain if you have any meaningful amount of data (and thus a large file)

Other problems with this application:
- It is unstable, crashing regularly.
- It "forgot" dozens if not hundreds of renaming rules. The rules are all still there -- Quicken just doesn't use them, anymore. So, the first few dozen times you update transactions in Quicken 2014, expect to see lots of entries like "SUZIES CARDS AND GIF929387 SOMEWHEREUSA".
- It is essentially impossible to copy text from or paste text into a transaction -- Quicken thinks you are trying to copy or paste the entire transaction, not just the selected or copied text.
- Online updates seem even slower than in previous versions, and render the application totally useless until they are completed. At least in prior versions, you could click on an account or tab and "kind of" work with the application while it updated your accounts; that's not even possible in this version.
- The new mobile app only works if you actively and consciously update your information to the "Quicken Cloud." Unlike the countless other applications out there that update seamlessly, in real time, without user intervention, Quicken requires you to take action to update your data.
- The new mobile app is basically garbage, anyway. It only displays the most basic information: "Cash" (counting all checking and savings accounts) and "Credit Debt." It gives some extremely high-level information about recent cash flow, but no detail. In the "Cash" and "Credit Debt" areas, it simply lists all of your accounts, sorted from highest balance to lowest. I mean ALL accounts, including accounts that are marked closed and "do not show in lists" in Quicken. I have been using Quicken for many years, while living in multiple countries. So, in my case, the mobile app lists far more closed accounts than active ones. I am actually going to uninstall the mobile app this evening, because it is far less useful than many other apps available for free.
- The projected balances feature is still very naive and refuses to estimate things like credit card payments at all beyond the next payment due, unless you set reminders on the basis of an estimated value (rather than scheduling a bill to pay the full amount).
- Investment analysis is still very weak.
- Extremely sluggish UI -- very hard to get going when you first open the app or go into a different account or tab. I launched it when I started writing this review and, as I type these words, it finally opened up the default view.
- The budgeting features are still basically useless.
- Still no built-in support for loans which accrue simple interest, rather than compound interest. Most student loans are non-compounding, at least if you are not in default, so this means that it isn't really worth your time to set up those accounts as loans in Quicken; you will end up manually typing the principal and interest values every single month.
- Still no ability to connect to many loan servicers, particularly for student loans. Other applications -- many of them free and including Intuit's own Mint -- can do this. It is absurd that a $100 application used by millions of people can't handle this yet.

This program is terrible. I will never be buying another version of Quicken, but am actively looking for a replacement. Recommendation: RUN AWAY.

It is quite possible that at one point Quicken was as good, but the current product is a nightmare of epic proportions. It would appear that after obviously cornering the market, Intuit has done nothing to leverage that into a superior product, instead it degrades with nothing of value left to compare it to. Here is a case where the free market has failed.

May I remind everyone, it is pretty simple: a date, a description, a credit or debit amount. And yet, this basic idea is lost in a maze of complexity inundated with failures.

While I find he interface poorly designed, a legacy set of junk that appears to have grow over the years such that the basics have fallen through the cracks, I need not waste my time on looking there. Why? Because I can't get my data in, nor trust what is there will be useful in the future.

To start, bringing in any of the history we all have requires one to jump though creative nightmarish hoops, for which the result is crap shoot (in the end I made a new \\"cash account\\" and imported one account at a time there and \\"cut 'n paste\\" into other accounts). Should one get in (either via luck with importing games or by throwing in the towel and abandoning your history), anything goes wrong and you are at the mercy of losing everything due to the complexity. Here, after 30 years of programming, I am entitle to jump to conclusions here about the cause: legacy complexity of too many esoteric features overwhelming the basics.

The most important point of a product like this is to gather this simple information from all the varied account interfaces (checking, savings, credit cards, brokerage, retirement) into one central interface. Yet institutional integration is hit or miss, with neither institutions nor Intuit caring.

Face it: no one is going to type in all their transactions. So, you darn well better be sure your institution works with Quicken or it will be useless. And, when it breaks, do not expect a fix - you are back to manual. This is the Achilles heel: you can't trust it with your history because you don't know what will happen tomorrow.

My conclusions are based on my own experience. My Bank Account would not download until after about 20 useless emails with support over 1 month, where they barely read anything I wrote. In the end I found the problem with Quicken (could not handle two accounts on one institution with the same \\"account name\\") by learning about and deciphering the Quicken logs I had sent them. After this they did not care about knowing this shortcoming. And the, one of my three credit cards that was supported was sold to another company without my consent... not supported any longer, and so now what do I do with that history and future? My conclusions are further supported by searching and finding that this is the same for zillions. How can it be that a company with a Monopoly in this market space gets mediocre and less reviews from most users? It is embarrassing.

There are many of you that use Quicken and have settled into a routine since you were lucky enough to find \\"things that worked\\". More power to you. But it is just a matter time before it goes bad for you. Probably the next \\"forced\\" upgrade, and/or when your financial institution is sold to another in this current way Wall St works.

As for new users considering this product: good luck, maybe you to will get\\"in\\". But, again, your future is dismal.

And for all of us, there is no hope in view. We are worse off than a decade ago, and with each release Quicken deteriorates as shown by intelligent reviews of those who have been with it for years. Alternatively Mint is barely holding on, for those willing to trust all their data to the \\"Mint\\" server which could go offline any time just like Intuit's previous online money site \\"Quicken Online\\".

One practical conclusion: at this price range don't expect to have all the bells and whistles. You will have to buy or download additional plugins and, for that purpose, you can read the recommendations found on sos or music radar sites. A daw is like a car, after chosing the model you have to look at the accompanying or offered packages. In music additional plugins can be quite expensive but you can find free plugins that you need. Happy hunting.

When I went to the Intuit website to look for a solution, I got sent in circles to user support forums (my least favorite way of handling customer support) and to the Intuit homepage. I couldn't find any links for live chat or a toll-free number for phone support. I finally gave up in frustration. When I started looking for instructions on how to get a refund, again I got sent in circles. The refund process is needlessly cumbersome. The message comes through loud and clear that Intuit doesn't care about its customers and that once you buy this lousy software, you are stuck with it. Finally I just deleted the software and chalked this one up to bitter experience. Avoid this software like the plague! If your money management needs are fairly simple, as mine are, you'll probably be better off with simple checkbook and budgeting spreadsheets that you can download and use for free and use with your favorite word processor or office suite.

I tried Quicken many many years ago and decided I liked Microsoft Money better. But a few years ago, Money basically went into sunset mode and updates through MS Money were no longer possible. So I tried Quicken. So disappointing is the online capabilities of Quicken. While it's nice to at least have SOME accounts online-capable, what makes Quicken more disappointing than Microsoft Money is the fact that even the transaction files you download from various financial websites are simply not readable by Quicken, even though they are readable by Money, such as the QIF files. Money will import QIF files and OFX files easily. Quicken does not recognize either one. It seems to only recognize its own format, and if the website you use for handling finances doesn't have a specific Quicken file, you'll end up entering transactions manually or searching the internet for methods you can use to alter the downloaded transaction file to trick Quicken into importing the data anyway.

Quicken's reasoning for not allowing the normal import of any QIF file is highly annoying and it seems to have no point. They simply don't allow QIF data to be imported into credit accounts, while MS Money does.

I expected more than this from Quicken, especially after all these years. I expected it to be compatible with at least one format from every website that offers transaction downloads, even from the site itself as an import file, but this is not the case at all. I have more financial sites that are incompatible with Quicken than I had with MS Money. What a shame.

That said, Quicken's ability to generate reports seems more robust than MS Money. Money would not show how much available credit you have on credit cards, but Quicken does. The text reports in Quicken are not as fancy-looking as the ones in MS Money, so visually, Quicken's reports seem to be ONLY about the numbers.

The graphical user interface seems slow. While I have a 6-core AMDVishera CPU, a GeForce GTX 650, and 16 GB of RAM on an Asus Crosshair V Formula Z motherboard, Quicken's speed of redrawing the screen makes it look like it's running on an old 386 computer. Paying one bill from the Bill Reminder screen can take about three seconds to finally enter and change all the data on the screen.

Sometimes all transactions don't import into accounts. I've had a few instances where I've had to manually enter transactions I've downloaded because they didn't "register" into the Quicken account, yet they showed up on the statement.

Another minus to this is that during reconciliation of accounts, some of the items you need to check off won't show up in the reconciliation screen. If you switch back to your register, you see that the transaction is actually there. Apparently Quicken does you a "favor" and limits the transactions displayed in the reconciliation screen by using the date range of the statement you're reconciling. If a transaction in the Quicken register is outside the date of the statement, there's some special click procedure you have to use on the context menu for the entry to change some hidden date that does not appear in the register itself, but changing that date to something that's within the statement's date range makes the transaction available for reconciliation.

Overall, there are a lot of very stupid characteristics of this financial software that seem to have no point, such as the one I just described, that make this software annoying. The only reason to use it is if you want something current that'll download at least some of your transactions from within the software itself. If you've got something that works the way you want it to now, stick with it.

That being said and not being that wise, I will plunge ahead and give you those first impressions.

Lightroom 5 is software that has a fairly considerable learning curve in that it is not immediately obvious what it does or how to make the best use of it. That, I suppose, is a contradiction, but that's the way I see it so far. To make things a bit clearer, once you have your photograph or digital graphics loaded in and you switch to the Develop mode, you're ready to rock simply by pushing this and pulling that and clicking on this and that and suddenly you begin to see just how much subtle power this program has in transforming your photograph or your digital graphic into something better than when it started. This is an OK product. I have used both PowerDirector 12 and PowerDirector 13. They are better than the entry-level free movie software bundled with a Mac or a typical PC, but I found them inferior to comparable Sony video editing software packages.

I prefer the Sony Vegas line of products (including both Vegas and Movie Studio) to the PowerDirector line. I find that there is far greater control and far more intuitive control in the comparable Sony software.

I like to play around with ideas - linking some shots (especially background shots) and seeing what works and then moving them around to get the timing and the sequence right. PowerDirector was far less forgiving for this sort of an editing style.

One example of a feature that I found annoying among the PowerDirector line of products is that in other software, if you set up a cross fade and then pull the two cross-faded items apart (e.g. to place another scene in between them), then they separate as distinct clips. But I found that when I cross-faded two clips in PowerDirector, the cross fade was permanent, in the sense that then ends of each of the two clips would be 'contaminated' with the cross faded material from the other clip. So you could not separate them and put something else in-between without removing the cross faded clips from the media tray and re-importing a clean copy of each clip for use.

After trying the PowerDirector line of products, I returned to the Sony video-editing products.

The download using broadband took about two hours, and installation after that took about two hours for a full install. The Ultimate version consists of [[ASIN:B00CA28J1I VideoStudio Pro X6 EN Mini-Box]] plus several plug-ins that enhance the product. The download includes separate installation media for Pro and the plug-ins, so you can choose what you want to install if you don't want everything that is included.

One disappointment is with registration of the product with Corel. Until the program is registered and a confirmation code is entered, a prompt is opened every time the program is opened to goad you to register the product, but the means that the program offers to register are not functioning. There are two choices given: to register from within the program, or to register using a web browser. Both methods attempt to contact a registration server that seems to be broken. When you try using a web browser a page opens that says that the site is \\"temporarily\\" unavailable, but it seems to be permanently unavailable. A few attempts opening the page have resulted in an error indicated that code running on the server is causing a server error, that normally happens with the code is buggy, or resources on the server are not permissioned correctly.

It is possible to create an account directly on the Corel website, and register the program with its serial number, but a confirmation code is not sent when that is done, so it does not help to get rid of the registration prompt. The Corel Guide that documents some of the functionality of the program is also depending on that code, so that is unavailable as well.

Perhaps that will be fixed after a little while, and registration can be completed normally. If that happens I'll try to remember to update my review. Don't hold your breath. These kinds of problems seem to stick around a long time with companies like Corel.

[Edit: This appears to have been resolved now, so registration is not a problem.]

Another problem exists with the proDAD plug-ins included with the Ultimate version. The first time each is accessed within the program an error message appears indicating that one of the DLL files for the plugin could not be loaded. Instructions are given in the error message from proDAD, but it is difficult to understand. It seems to require purchase of the full versions of the plug-ins. I have not been able to get the proDAD plug-ins to work so far.

[Edit: I have a ticket open with Corel for this problem. They have asked for a lot of information about my system, which I have given, so I am now waiting to see if they can provide a fix. According to the Corel user forums Corel is supposed to be working on a hot fix for the issue, but that note was from last June.]

I have also found that VideoStudio does not play well with all video formats. I may be able to convert these to another format that works better within the program, but I have not tried doing that yet.

Other than problems like this the program is not difficult to use, especially if you have used video editing software before. The interface is similar to other programs such as [[ASIN:B00B02JP44 Camtasia Studio - ( v. 8 ) - complete packa]] with three main window panes, a video scrubbing area (where you can view video media), a timeline where media are assembled and modified, and a browser area where media and special effects can be selected and configured.

The program has a great deal of flexibility when it comes to its interface. The window panes can be docked to or removed from the main window and moved around however you wish to take advantage of your screen space as much as possible. If you have multiple monitors this allows you to utilize the monitors more efficiently. With two monitors you might move the timeline to a monitor by itself and maximize it there, and have the scrubber and browser maximized in the other monitor.

It has options to read video from video players, and digital, and analog cameras (a capture device of some kind is required for the latter), and even a screen capture program to help with the production of program tutorials and other types of output. The screen capture tool provides options for capturing audio from a microphone, and system audio, and to animate mouse clicks. You can select only one audio input unfortunately, but that is an annoyance, but of course you can add audio later while editing your production.
