Let me start by pointing out that I just bought this product and I haven't used it other than to install it and take a quick look through its options.

That said, I have Corel PaintShop Pro X5 and Adobe Photoshop Elements 11. I use PaintShop Pro extensively, mainly to retouch downloaded images for genealogy purposes and also scanned yearbook pages and cleanup of document images. In other words, I don't do photography, I don't do from-scratch image creation, and I don't use artistic effects. But I have enough experience to be able to look through menu options, etc., and recognize what PhotoStudio can do and what is missing compared to Elements and PaintShop.

The suggested retail price of PhotoStudio, PaintShop and Elements are very similar and often PaintShop is available for less than PhotoStudio's discounted price. (PaintShop comes in two versions: 1) PaintShop Pro [Photo] and 2) PaintShop Pro Ultimate. Both have the same PAINTSHOP program but Ultimate includes additional effects filters and brushes and standalone old versions of third-party programs.)

Regarding functionality, Elements is best, then PaintShop, with PhotoStudio a DISTANT third.

Regarding ease of use FOR COMPLEX ACTIVITIES it looks like PaintShop and PhotoStudio are similar. I find Elements confusing and less intuitive, but I'm not an image-editing \\"power user\\". A major advantage of Elements is that because it is basically \\"Photoshop Junior\\", there are LOADS of video tutorials and books available. There are also quite a few video tutorials for PaintShop but many fewer books.

It looks like there isn't much in the way of either video tutorials or books for PhotoStudio. HOWEVER, because PhotoStudio has much less functionality, tutorials for either Elements or PaintShop can easily be applied. At most the keystrokes might change. Also, a user who would buy PhotoStudio rather than PaintShop or Elements will be doing much more basic activities.

\\"Help\\" is minimal. It is basically HTML and only has a VERY basic description of the function. There is no \\"search\\" option. There are no tooltips.

There are no auto-correct options such as correct perspective distortion or \\"straighten\\", where you put the ends of a line at two points and click \\"Make horizontal\\" (or \\"Make vertical\\") and the program automatically tilts the entire image. \\"Preferences\\" only has 3 options: 1) set number of undo levels, 2) location of the cache folder, and 3) set the appearance of the transparency background. I don't see a \\"feathering\\" option for paste, where the program automatically blends the color of the \\"to be pasted\\" block to match the color of the target area better and make the paste less noticeable.

PhotoStudio is really NOT a \\"general purpose\\" editor. It's aimed at the elementary-to-intermediate user who mainly wants to touch up photos of people. THE reason I bought it is the FACE BEAUTIFY feature. Search YouTube for \\"ArcSoft PhotoStudio Face Beautify\\" and \\"PaintShop Pro Makeover\\". Although PaintShop, Elements and PhotoStudio all have the tools to do makeovers, PhotoStudio's are MUCH more automated and intuitive for the casual user.

PhotoStudio does support layers but not masks. It does not support CMYK, HSL or channels.

Under Windows 7, PaintShop Pro X5 shows an installed size of 154MB and Elements shows 2.59GB. PhotoStudio doesn't show a size in Windows Add/Delete Programs but the installer is 38MB and C:\Program Files shows 28MB.

To be an \\"image-editing power user\\" you'll want Elements. For \\"intermediate-to-borderline-advanced\\" you'll want PaintShop. (Also, PaintShop has script recording and Elements doesn't.) Summary: I was hoping my difficulties with Q13 were simply a matter of getting used to a new version......but quite frankly, I regret having bought it. I have used Quicken for over 20 years and I have loved the program. It used to be so intuitive to use. Q13 is useable for home and business accounting, but it is no longer easy. If you are new to home accounting programs... please be warned, this one is NOT user friendly. As Quicken has added more options; the program has become overly cumbersome.

Details: I `upgraded' and `downgraded' simultaneously. Previously was using Quicken Home & Business 2009; bought and downloaded Quicken Deluxe 2013 in April. This has been an experience.

Registers: I find the print size very large, and apparently not adjustable, which results in seeing a lower number of transactions at a time. This can be quite annoying. There are also a lot of colors in this version. I hate to say this, but when dealing with numbers perhaps a black&white or shades of gray color options would be good.

Planning: The retirement planning tab works well. Just remember that the answers you see are totally dependent upon the numbers you use (GIGO). The program will give you suggestions, ex: I chose a rate of return of 3% for a 401K... the program felt that was very low... it obviously has not been out there over the last 5 years watching its retirement funds plummet. lol Be careful of the assumptions used in the calculations, however on the plus side you can get access to those assumptions and change them in the program.

Budgeting: Creating a budget has been a lot of work. My suggestion is that you print out your current budget from your current version of Quicken BEFORE you upgrade to Q13. Then get rid of anything Q13 automatically sets up as a budget... it will cause you more heartache than you can imagine. Start your new budget from scratch using your paper copy. I guarantee you will also find yourself using Q community help a lot. Q13 follows different rules than the previous Q versions with budgeting. I found myself unable to get budgets to add correctly (isn't this a math program??); when they did, the reports would not add. As an example, I set up my normal category of \\"Taxes\\" with sub-categories for \\"Federal\\", \\"State\\", \\"Soc Sec\\", etc. I set a budget category group of \\"Tax\\" to include the \\"Taxes\\" category and its subs. I found that the subs would automatically rollup and sum into the \\"Taxes\\" category (as they should)...... then the parent \\"Taxes\\" would rollup to the top category group \\"Tax\\" (as it should).... but the subcategories also rolled up to the top category group \\"Tax\\"...(resulting in the top category group of \\"Tax\\" being double the amount it should be). There's a fix to the problem that includes resetting everything to \\"0\\" then rebudgeting at this link: [...]
but why am I working this hard for a simple budget? Like any program, its all about understanding the rules. But... I would not term this program `user friendly'.

Converting Home & Business to Deluxe: The conversion from H&B to Dlx went rather well for accounts and transactions. I was impressed that it was able to convert invoices, etc from H&B, I did not think they would be supported in Q13. I have not yet opened any previously saved reports; and based upon what I have read at the Q community help...I will not. Apparently, Q13 has difficulty with saved reports from previous Q Deluxes..., there's no use my even trying from an H&B. Hopefully, I still have the old H&B disk somewhere.

Mobile App: I don't have a smart phone, so this was not a deciding factor for me. With the trouble it's given me on a computer....I would not bet on the mobile app.

I have been using MS Office products since the early 90s. I have always loved using MS Office and cannot imagine life without it. As a teacher I rely heavily on Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, especially.

The computers at school have Office 2010 on them, and I love all of the newer features. In particular, the ability to insert videos into PowerPoint presentations is especially usefully to me as a Social Studies teacher. Unfortunately, my school only has the license to provide us with a copy of Office 2003 to install on our personal computers for home use. Since I love all of the newer features, I decided to buy and install the latest version of MS Office on my personal laptop. Big mistake.

I bought the Office Home and Student version, not Office 365. Yes, I got all of the great new features, but all of those benefits are cancelled out by the one main drawback of the new version--the inability to work offline. Yes, that's right--you cannot use this version of office unless you are connected to the internet. So when I'm at work and cannot connect my personal laptop to the internet, Office is totally useless to me. Or, if I am travelling or away from my house, I'm out of luck. I cannot believe Microsoft thought this was a good idea. I have read many complaints on line and confirmed this is a widespread issue. Like many people, I believe this is a digital rights/copy protection scheme, and I don't buy Microsoft's denial.

The inability to use this program without an internet connection is a huge problem for me. Often, I would like to open and run a PowerPoint from my laptop at work, but I can't. Even worse, if I am trying to get work done at home and the internet is down for some reason, I am out of luck.

Another super-annoying problem caused by the inability to work off-line is that I will be working on something and then the program stops working and tells me \\"Office may appear unresponsive\\" because it is streaming necessary files. This happens every time I am using MS Office. It will start working again after some time, but I often lose my train of thought or get distracted by something else during this time. It is crazy that I have to deal with an issue like this on a program I paid a whole lot of money for.

As a result of these drawbacks of Office 2013, I am only giving this product two stars. If I could work off line and didn't have to wait for files to stream all the time, I would have given this product five stars. I strongly encourage people to buy or stick with an older version of Office. I will definitely not buy a newer version of Office until this issue is fixed. I cannot say enough how much I have always loved Office and how many hours I have used Word, Outlook, Excel, and PowerPoint. It really makes me sad and disappointed to think I will either have to stick with an old program or find an different one to use. I am to the point where I am going to install Office 2003 and use that one instead. My only hope is that Microsoft will wake up and look at all of the complaints on the internet and come out with an update that allows their loyal customers to use the product we paid for when and where we want.

And to save Microsoft from posting a useless reply to this message, I have their forums and even posted a question about this problem. Predictably, my question got no response. Here's that thread:

[...]

I just tried again to open word while wifi is off and my laptop is in airplane mode, and a dialog box pops up with this message:

\\"Background installation ran into a problem.
Please make sure you're still connected to the internet, or try connecting to a different network.
We'll automatically resume installation as soon as possible, and you can keep working once we do.\\"

Microsoft's answer in the forum was that once all files are installed, we should be able to work while in airplane mode, but this is not true. I have had this program on my computer since February, I have used it for many hours, and this still happens 100% of the time. I also saw a moderator on the forum as why we would want to work offline, which is an outlandish question to ask. I explained why above. Sometimes we don't have a choice.

Like I said, my hope here is not to get a refund, but that Microsoft will come to its senses and not drive off countless loyal customers by adding pointless, dumb features to MS Office.

I recently purchased a new computer and needed an office suite for it. Rather than purchase another copy of MS Office, I thought I would try Corel's WordPerfect office suite. It was fairly priced and it was easy to download. Also, WordPerfect used to be THE word processing program years ago (before Windows). The look-and-feel is dated and it just doesn't look right. Also, the look of the "hidden characters" (like the "space" and the paragraph symbols), when visible, is out-of-proportion and somewhat jarring. I've also had a few minor glitches with saving and opening files, and this does not give me confidence in the stability of the programs. At this point, I prefer OpenOffice over WordPerfect office.

I'm sure others have had positive results and like the program. More power to them! But if I had to recommend a non-MS Office suite at this time, I would recommend OpenOffice over WordPerfect office. Sorry Corel!

I'll continue to experiment with WordPerfect office. If I change my mind, I'll revise/update this review.

I'm a relatively new user to this program, so this isn't a definitive review but rather a "first impressions".  There seems to be a lot to like in terms of features, capabilities, and quality of results. But it's really, really hard to get past just how clunky the user interface is. Some examples:  1) This is really a program for working on a single image. Although it does include a "browser" that lets you pick the image to be edited from a folder, the browser is slow and doesn't really add any value.  2) For Raw files, first you pick the white balance setting, then you open the file. If you don't like the result, you close the file, pick another white balance setting, then reopen the file. Repeat until you're mostly happy. Virtually every other editing program lets you adjust the white balance while you're seeing how it affects the image. Almost every other editing program gives you an "eyedropper" you can use on a neutral point in the image to set the white balance, but not this one. Also, white balance is purely color temperature, with no ability to adjust the magenta/green axis.  3) There is no Undo. This is a non-destructive editor, so it's certainly possible to go back and reset things by hand as long as you remember how they used to be set, but a lot of times it's just easier to hit CTRL-Z to undo a mistake or an experiment. Not here. CTRL-Z takes you to the last "restore point" you create by hitting SHIFT-Z. If you haven't created a restore point, CTRL-Z has no effect.  4) You always have to start from one of the presets. You can create your own Custom preset that has no initial effect and use that as a starting point, but should that really be necessary to do?  5) Before/after comparison is limited to a small window with a movable divider. That's not unheard-of, but most editors provide a button you can press to momentarily show the Before image.  6) There's no preview for the "effects" (the adjustment layers that make the changes). To see if you want to use a particular effect, you have to add it and then, if you didn't want it, you delete it. Deleting an effect always requires clicking "Yes" on a confirmation dialog and there's no way to turn off that confirmation. Since there are 85 effects to choose from, this gets old really fast.  7) Cropping is only available during saving. Cropping is completely free-form and by eye; there are no presets for particular aspect ratios, no way to set a specific crop size, and no way to determine what pixel sizes you're cropping to.  For the photographer who just wants to make his pictures look "true to life" or "slightly better than real life," there's not much here that isn't available in more established products that have a much more pleasant user interface. Also, as the name suggests, Franzis COLOR Projects provides only minimal capabilities for producing black-and-white images (Franzis offers two other programs for that purpose).  The creative, especially the professional creative tasked with producing color images that project a particular ambiance, flair, or emotional impact, might well find Franzis COLOR Projects to be worth the hassle. It's capable of an incredibly wide range of creative "looks," and those looks seem to be very nicely done. Learning one's way around the 85 effects and their respective controls, 84 preset settings, and 35 color-film emulations is going to take a fair amount of time and dedication.

To understand the problem, you'll need a quick back story into modern computer displays

Many modern computers are now using 1080HD monitors, which is great! you can watch movies and videos in glorious as real as it gets HD. The problem this created was that text and menus in windows started to get really small, because a 100 pixel menu, on a full HD screen would be an invisible spec. But on an old 800x600 screen, would be a large billboard.
The fix for this problem is something called DPI-scaling or a DPI modifier. All it means is that you take menus and text, and make them bigger. If you simply did this by lowering the resolution of the screen, the quality would no longer be HD, defeating the point of even having an HD screen.

99.999999999999999% of applications made in the last 15-20 years support, and work great with this feature. As company's that make these programs have been aware that screen resolution has always been increasing since the dawn of computers and have programmed for this eventuality.
However, the programmers for this are in the very very small minority of stupid idiots, who couldn't possibly comprehend this.

Simply put, most (if not all) windows 7 & later computers come out of the box running 125% DPI. Because with today's screens, you wouldn't be able to see anything without it set that way. This program is completely incompatible with that setting, things will be cut off and you won't really be able to use it. What is even more irritating, is that the program tells you it won't work with that setting, which means the programmers were aware of the issue, and too lazy or cheep to fix it! so you have 3 ways to deal with this, but none of them truly 'fix' the problem.

A. Turn off your DPI setting, and live with the fact that you will never be able to see anything on the computer screen without a magnifying glass.

B. Disable a setting in windows called \\"Use Windows XP style DPI scaling\\". This will make this program work fine, although it will be blurry. HOWEVER, be warned that this setting can cause LOTS of other programs on your computer that have worked fine before, to get all messed up and blurry and look like crap. (if you want to do this, just Google the setting & you can find out how)

C. Right click on Resume Maker's short-cut, click properties, click compatibly. then check \\"Disable visual themes\\" and \\"Disable display scaling on high DPI settings\\". This will not fix everything, but it will help reduce some of the text cut off, but the misplaced buttons and awkward layout issues remain.

The only real way for this to be fixed, is for the developer to go back and do a relatively easy fix of the interface. But I wouldn't count on it, since they were too lazy to program it with this simple thing in the first place.

Also, an important thing to note: MICROSOFT HAS MARKED THIS AS A WINDOWS INCOMPATIBLE PROGRAM, because of this issue.

Level Set: As many others here, I've been a long-time Quicken user. I'm reasonably techically savvy having worked as a software developer for 30+ years and have been a PC owner since 1982. In years gone by, Quicken was an outstanding application. When lots of applications at that time were fraught with operational and especially, human factor, problems, Quicken was a marvel of reliability and operational ease -- way ahead of the curve. Things have changed since then.

Again, as many others, I updated from Quicken 2010 only because of the pending cessation of online banking support. I purchased Premier 2013 and downloaded it from Amazon. As an aside, I've always been pleased with the service from Amazon, and the problems I note here are unrelated to Amazon.

Installation has been one problem after another. Unfortunately I didn't keep completely detailed notes of the activity, so my description of the activity will be a bit hit and miss.

The download consists of a small installer which then actually loads the main Quicken executable. This download process completed without problems, although it did take quite a bit longer than I would have expected via my relatively capable broadband connection.

Upon completion of the download, the installation began. The installation consists of three steps which are monitored on the display:
Uninstall of the existing Quicken,
Install of 2013, and
Install of 2013 updates.

Install of 2013 updates never completed -- just hung near the end. No way to easily recover. Couldn't cancel. Had to reboot via task manager.

After restart, clicked on Quicken Premier 2013 desktop icon (which had gotten installed) and got message saying downloaded executable could not be found, and I needed to redownload from the Amazon library which I did. Eventually reloaded and same problem occurred with the \\"Install 0f 2013 Updates\\" portion not completing. Sometime during this process I saw an error messages saying \\"Quicken failed to install FIDIR.TXT, a required online banking setup file. Please reinstall Quicken. If problem persists, contact Quicken support.\\"
I tired to do this , but discovered that Quicken support is available only Mon-Fri 5 am to 5 pm.

Searched around the web and saw a reference to FIDIR.TXT sometimes not being activated because of a permission problem. The reference further indicated that the file resides in Program Data/Intuit/Quicken/Common/...(I forget the rest of the folder name). I looked there and indeed discovered that I did not have permission to see the file. Messed around with advanced permissions for a bit and eventually was able to modify the permission appropriately.

I tried the reinstall again, and it eventually worked. (there very likely were other intervening problems which I since forgotten).

I restarted the application and, at least superficially, it appeared to be operational. While looking around, I saw an indication on the display that I should update to R10. I looked in \\"About Quicken\\" and discovered I was at R2. So I clicked on the update to load/install R10 and the system sat there for the longest time giving no indication that anything was happening. After about 10 minutes I had enough and either just cancelled or rebooted (don't remember which).

Restarted Quicken and again saw the indication about updating to R10. Tried again. Same thing -- system just sat there with no indication that anything was happening. After another long period of waiting, I was about to abort the operation when -- out of the blue --the system responded that the operation was complete! Rechecked \\"About Quicken\\" and -- wonder of wonders -- I was finally at R10.

Spent a few minutes more looking at the application and it seems to be operating correctly. We'll see what happens over the next few days/weeks. If anything significant transpires, I'll update this review.

Net: Far too many installation problems. In the old days, Intuit produced an outstanding product. At this point, they're fortunate there is not a reasonable alternative.

Since getting all the initial install problems sorted out, the application has been running satisfactorily -- up until now. When I started it last night it indicated the R11 was now available and suggested that I install it. I tried multiple times to do this with various problems. Most times the d/l and install appeared to complete properly (although with a completely non-informative progress bar), but \\"About Quicken\\" still shows that I'm running R10 and I continue to get the \\"Update to R11\\" notification. Very disappointing and frustrating.

One of my New Year's resolutions this year was to start getting serious about my budget.  Most of the people in my family seem to manage their money well, but I have never stuck to a long-term budget or really definitively outlined my financial goals.  I decided to make a budget.  Then, I realized that tracking financial transactions would be key to making wise spending/saving/investment decisions.  I decided to buy Quicken ($60 is what they charge for the Deluxe Edition on their website - they do not sell the Starter Edition.)  I got directed to Amazon and, funny, just happened to have a $25 gift card that I got as a door gift at our holiday party - so, this cost me $.57 out of my own pocket.  I think that might give you some perspective as you read this.    Positives:  This program is significantly less expensive than most.  It does not make you overpay for features you might not need.  If you do not own a home, do not have investments, have sophisticated needs, etc., then you should be pretty happy based on the value.  This program syncs with your bank account and gives you a record of all of your transactions.  This hasn't been problem free, but it is a pretty solid system overall.  It pretty accurately codes your debit card transactions by category - things like housing, food (and alcohol), auto, insurance, health, entertainment, etc.  You can also go back and review certain categories and sub-categories, which makes catching any categorization errors an easy task.  You can apparently have several accounts - I've only entered one so far, and I believe that you can input your charge cards as well, although I have yet to do that.  This is a good tool for tracking spending and seeing where your money goes.  It also allows you to set-up budget by category and compare it to your spending.  I need to explore it more.  So, definitely some good stuff for the price.    Negatives:  I feel like the program's interface could have been better.  There were a few things thatseemed a bit counter-intuitive in the navigation.  I mentioned above that I haven't explored the budget features much, mainly because they don't seem all that great.  I don't really budget by the month - I think of everything in 2 or 4 (or 6, twice a year) week cycles.  I don't seem to see a way to switch to the proper time frame.  I also found that the recurring budget/pay reminder system seemed to have all of the functionality of a square wheel.  Reminders don't go away.  They are somehow involved in transaction register yet can't be tied to the others that can be downloaded from your bank account.  On that topic, the bank account download feature ended up fouling once because I changed the name of an account in my view.  I figured that wouldn't effect your connection, but apparently my bank couldn't sync after that.  I deleted it and started again, and now everything in fine.  However, I have to go back and redo a bunch of the categorization errors (also, specified transactions, but that shouldn't be more than 30-40 minutes.  In the scheme of things, probably not that big a deal considering the price of the software.  I also wasn't thrilled that my bank account balance was constantly different than my actual cash on hand as displayed based on what I've entered.  I believe they just chose a random day and started from there, so things don't add up.  I need to determine how to reconcile the difference.  I also don't get why I have to wait an extra day to download transactions that I can see in my online banking.  And, it usually takes a few hours after I update my accounts in Quicken to be able to log back in to my online banking.      Overall:  Solid C.  I spent $.57.  I am not disappointed.  I would have wasted the card on Kindle books (sorry, Amazon...) if I hadn't bought this software.  I've enjoyed a lot about it.  I really like the spending tracking. Quickbooks online plus is a fantastic product, however it can get a little pricey. For example, I've owned quickbooks pro for a number of years, and always upgrade after 2-3 years (the most recent version I've owned is quickbooks pro 2014). With quickbooks online, you have to pay a monthly (or yearly if you choose) subscription price, where as the desktop version is yours to own forever. The amazon price is good for a year only, but after that you'll be at the mercy of intuit's price However, if you believe you'll upgrade every year anyways then it might be worth it. Looking beyond pricing, here are the features I've found most useful in quickbooks online:

1. It lives on the cloud: It allows me to work in the office & at home, without lugging my laptop around (this was what I used to do when I had the desktop version). With quickbooks online, you can access your company file from any computer with an internet connection (and there is no software to install). This also means your data is backed up and safe every time.

2. Mobile App: Quickbooks online also has a mobile app that can be downloaded for your iPhone (not sure about android or windows). While I believe the iPhone app is still a little basic, it does help me save time. For example, if I'm in the field and I incur an expense (i.e. we buy our workers lunch) I can take a picture of the receipt, enter the amount, payee, select what kind of expense it was from my chart of accounts, assign the expense to a class (I make heavy use of the class tracking feature because it lets me track income for each of my rental properties separately). After I click done, the expense posts right away (which means I don't have to save the receipt and enter it when I'm in front of a computer.

3. I save time entering transactions: I have my checking & credit card accounts connected to it. Quickbooks makes matching transactions that you've entered to a bank or credit card charge a snap. For example, ifI buy food using my credit card and enter the expense either through my phone or the computer, quick books will let you match that transaction to the charge on your credit card statement. This makes reconciliation go by much much faster.

Overall: If you own quickbooks pro desktop and are considering upgrading, I'd strongly suggest you use the thirty day trial intuit offers to setup a sample company and play around with it. A lot of the features & terms are the same as quickbooks desktop, however the layout is a little bit different and you do have to play with the settings to make it suit your custom needs.
If you've never owned quickbooks before, then I would recommend the online version. My review is for quickbooks online plus, but you're needs might be met by quickbooks online simple start or essentials which are a little cheaper. Intuit has a comparison chart so you can see which edition has the features you need.

I've used TurboTax for two decades to prepare my federal and state tax return. It does the job. For better or worse, I'm used to it. Yet it has needless weak points and provides needless annoyances.

VAGUE ERROR MESSAGES: When TurboTax checks for errors in your return, the messages explaining the possible errors are often hard to understand.

NAVIGATION: In preparing a long-form return on TurboTax, you will navigate through many, many pages (in my case, over 200). To reach the next page, you must go to the bottom of the current page and click \\"Continue.\\" But the \\"Continue\\" is hidden behind the Windows 7 taskbar (at least on my Lenovo Thinkpad), even on pages that contain only a few lines of text. You need to click on the page and scroll to the bottom before you can see and click \\"Continue.\\"

EXTRA CHARGE: TurboTax will charge you extra for e-filing your state return. It should disclose that charge clearly and specifically before you buy the product.

UPGRADES: Be wary of buying the many upgrades and additional services TurboTax will offer. Most users of TurboTax Deluxe will derive little additional benefit from them.

SELF-SERVING CHATTER: As you proceed through your return, you face recurring chatter implying that you owe your deductions and credits to TurboTax. It labels your total federal deductions, \\"federal deductions we found for you.\\" It labels your total state deductions, \\"state deductions we found for you.\\" As though you would have had no deductions or credits at all but for using TurboTax.

PERSONAL INFORMATION: When you first open this software, TurboTax demands a full page of contact information, including your mobile telephone number. It says it demands this information so it can notify you if the rules change. I provided all the requested information except my phone number. But that wasn't good enough for TurboTax. For the next ten or so times that I opened the software, it made me start withthe contact-information screen. I'd already given TurboTax my e-mail address; it didn't need my phone number. Once TurboTax has your phone number, it's free to make telemarketing calls. To prevent those calls, you need to go through the separate exercise of changing your contact preferences. And you can't do even that without giving TurboTax your daytime phone number.

I think Intuit did the right thing here. I'm glad they stepped up to the plate and are trying to appease customers!

Of course, I paid up each time only to be rewarded by a rocky upgrade to software that was even more buggy, even more bloated, even less friendly than before. But I digress...

This service is ordered through software -- so it wouldbe very simple to do a check of the required information against state policy and notify you when the state requires more information than they can provide. (By the way, I tried to look up the post on their forum from less than a year ago but it has been removed.)

Bottom Line: Intuit was a good company once, but has lost its way and has forgotten its customers. If you are a current Quicken user faced with a forced upgrade, version 2010 is better than at least, 2007. upgrade only when necessary. My upgrades this decade were in 2004 and 2007.

As a heavy user since 1988, I've seen a lot change with Quicken, many have been painful. Versions this decade are the least problematic. Periodic upgrades do make sense given its Internet centric operation because HTML, encryption, security protocols, and more, have evolved much and Quicken must adopt these changes. Alas, to users most of these are invisible and behind the scenes. In 2010, Quicken now uses the .NET framework for coding, a mixed blessing, as it consumes more memory, resources and disk space to add capability and stability. Computers should find these added needs inconsequential if these machines run games and 720p movies easily. I've not had problems with data syncing, slow response, bugs, lost data, corrupt files etc., despite my 4 year old computer and continuous data going back to 1985.

I've never upgraded to a first release of a new version to avoid bugs, nor overwrite a prior version. Always make a full system backup before installation, a system restore point just before installation, then a fresh install, then import the prior data file as a copy, keeping the old file intact. This leads to the least, if not problem free upgrade and an effortless path back to the old version should the upgrade bomb. Although I received 2010 Release 1.0, online files were available to upgrade my 2010 to Release 4.0.

The GUI design has remain unchanged, and clearly noticeable improvements and editing aids are welcome, BUT not worth paying for.

Quicken does make effortless a core function of personal finance, quick retrieval and reliable storage of data, editing and later analysis via reports. In the past decade, data retrieval has been nearly flawless; duplicate entries are increasingly rare even if you overlap a data set, say after syncing manually then later add data using a QFX file. However, Quicken has many shortcomings that should have been fixed decades ago. Quicken has sub-optimally organized or thought out functions. Its not intuitive where a function is, several do the same thing or are poorly thought out. For example, there are 3 ways to write electronic checks that do the same thing differently: through a 1990s \\"online banking\\" interface, the checking register, or a separate checkbook app. Attachments to register entries, such as jpgs of checks, can be encrypted individually, however you can see the files whether encrypted or not, the annunciator is poorly located so its not immediately clear if attachments are encrypted, and this option implies Quicken data files are not encrypted entirely, a serious oversight. There is also suggestion from Elcomsoft, that a backdoor exists for decoding Quicken data file passwords. Luckily, one can separately encrypt files or drive partitions using Windows options or 3rd party programs.

The new user or light Quicken user should know there are several free personal finance managers available for download that read Quicken formats. I've tried some of them but they lack Quicken's overall flexibility, and they are similar to early versions of Quicken. However, with the user manual, the tutorials, and Google searches for articles and help-boards, you can easily figure out how to use iBank. Here are a couple problems I solved, in case that will help anyone.

When you are creating your QIF data file to export from Quicken to iBank, make sure you select \\"all accounts\\" at the top of the drop down menu. Otherwise it will just transfer one account. (Quicken preselected just one account.) Also, when you first open your account in iBank, all the transactions will be cleared but not reconciled. To solve this, simply do a reconciliation that begins with your account's original opening date and balance and everything should easily reconcile. It took me less than ten minutes to figure this out and then reconcile my main checking account. Also, when I exported new transactions from my bank's website, using QFX files, iBank did not automatically open and allow me to import the file as described by iBank. I had to first save the QXF file and then go to the main menu and select either File or Account, then Import, and then the QXF file. But it was relatively fast once I figured it out. (Or you can pay for a subscription to iBank which will then will download your transactions automatically from all your banks.)

Next, edit the top check by dragging each section (date, payee, etc.) to where you want it. (The other two checks automatically adjust). When you move a section, you can see measurements (which now seem to be in inches - go figure) in small numbers above it. Both height and width measurements change as you drag. This was somewhat difficult. Just when you get the height right, it changes as you adjust the width placement. So, I'm a long time H&R Block Tax software customer. I've always been happy with the product, and the price - way less than TurboTax or a human. That said, I just battled a frustrating install process and finally figured out the problem. After installing 2013, the first order of business was to download a software update (Federal). The update downloaded, and then failed during update. The software went into this cycle of prompting for an update, failing to install it (would get to about 80% and then roll back), then prompting for an update again. After cycling through this a few times and failing, I uninstalled 2013, re-installed, and proceeded to battle the same issue.

After an hour of frustration I thought to myself, I wonder if having H&R Block 2012 on my machine is causing a problem? So, I uninstalled 2012, uninstalled 2013, then re-installed 2013 and voila, problem solved. So, if any of you out there have 2012 installed (or potentially any other version), and you are having install/update problems - I would remove previous versions first!

Software conflicts happen, I get it. The reason for the two-star review is because the conflict isn't addressed AT ALL by the 2013 software. The 2013 software should have checked for previous versions during install and prompted for removal. At minimum, a warning or disclaimer should have been provided with the product detailing this as part of the install instructions. At BARE MINIMUM, they would have posted something about this on their online support page. Considering they left me to battle this for an hour before eventually solving the problem on my own, I'm not real thrilled with them to start this year's tax season. This is disappointing because I generally start my taxes with a feeling of happiness, euphoria really - and they took this feeling of joy away from me...

Other comments are also correct about the unnecessary up-sell attempt to premium - before they even know if you NEED it and the fact that if you need to file a state return (I don't) be sure to pay the extra $$$ now and buy the version with state included - they charge more to bolt it on within the software.

I have a number of systems here, including desktops and laptops with varying types of connectivity. They range from old 700GHz P4 units up to recent, relatively fast quad-cores, and I run a range of different antivirus programs as well - under the theory that since no single solution is ever 100% up to date (as proven by the failure of each and every one of them to detect new threats that have gotten through in the past) it is wise to have several different methods of detection of malware on the network-connected systems. As a result, I've had Symantec's Norton Internet Security and the free versions of AVG and Avast in use for some time, and I recently added Kaspersky Internet Security on one of the most heavily-used machines. And I am annoyed to have to say that Kaspersky has, by far, proven to be the worst from a system performance hit standpoint. I will most likely swap the Kaspersky out for AVG or Symantec, or perhaps try one of the previously untested competitors, in the very near future. At present, Kaspersky has been running a full system scan on this machine for 11 hours, and it is only at 22% completion. Part of the problem appears to be that it stalls almost totally when it encounters something that it considers a threat that is inside of an archive of any kind; some old backups from a website that had been hit years ago with a worm triggered a warning earlier, and since I really didn't need those backups anymore, I told it to eliminate the threat. That was about an hour ago. Any minute now, it will pop up another dialog box telling me that it can't get rid of the threat without deleting the whole archive, to which I will reply by clicking on the "Delete" button, and it will take a good many minutes more for it to follow that instruction. I know this because I've already been through this lather-rinse-repeat cycle over both such infected-website-backup archives and some inbound emails that had trojans inside zips. Even with those far simpler emailed zipfile attachments (containing nothing *but* the malware) it took a long time for Kaspersky to deal with them. Its own internal update routines also seem to have issues; five days ago, Kaspersky complained that it needed to update itself (which seemed odd, since I had it configured to do that automatically) and the update stalled at 17% for more than 24 hours before I finally rebooted and restarted the process.

In short, this package seems to be unusually fragile and slow, appears to handle errors and detection-response procedures clumsily, and just generally fails to live up to the kind of standard that I had expected from what others had called a top-notch package. Your mileage may vary, but for me, this has not been a successful experiment.

I looked at alternatives to Quicken, but for all practical purposes Intuit currently has a lock on the market - nothing else comes close in terms of functionality and ease of use.    I am a sole practitioner attorney, so I was using Quicken 2008 Home & Business. However, the only business feature I ever used was the invoice account, and I determined I could do the same thing by creating an \\"accounts receivable\\" account in regular old Quicken (I did not print invoices from Quicken - just tracked them). Since I did not see the benefit of paying the premium to continue to have access to so-called business features that I did not need or use I downloaded Quicken 2011 Deluxe.    The Positive Experience Part: After reading all the bad reviews I was expecting some sort of problem, but it all went fine. The software downloaded quickly, removed Quicken 2008, retrieved all the fixes to Quicken 2011, and installed to my Windows 7 system without a hitch (note to those experiencing problems - you should ALWAYS make sure your Windows system has all the current updates). When I opened it, the software immediately found my old files (I have two - separate business and personal) and converted them. Everything appeared exactly as it did in Quicken 2008. I downloaded transactions from my bank, paid my bills, all hunky dorey.    I have not seen anything that says \\"upgrade\\" as opposed to \\"redesign,\\" but I like it so far. I like the fact that Quicken 2011 now uses one file instead of the three that Quicken 2008 used - I could never keep track of which was which. I also like the \\"See Where Your Money Goes\\" pie chart that quickly lets me get details about what I have been spending. I have not played with all the features, but from what I have looked at the redesign makes it simpler to find useful information.    Several purchasers complained about ads, but I don't see them. I clicked \\"later\\" (\\"never\\" was not an option) and it has not pestered me about it again.    So, overall, I would prefer that Intuit does not require me to spend $40+ every three years to buy new software when there is nothing wrong with the old, but I still think that Quicken is the best personal finance software available and will recommend the Deluxe version.

I'm a semi-truck driver, and needed a good mapping program. Compared to this program - Delorme Street Atlas USA (2014), Microsoft Streets and Trips is the better of the two.

I tested each by mapping a standard trip that I frequently make: from Sumner, WA to Great Falls, MT. My truck is governed at 62 mph, and I customarily drive this route in 10 hours and 50 minutes - a single day trip (DOT rules don't allow me to drive more than 11 hours). The trip is 651 miles.

Delorme maps this trip at 696.38 miles. It does not take the logical routes of WA-18 or MT-200, no matter which route setting I select ("Shortest" or "Quickest").

To follow the Delorme route would cost me 45 minutes, and I could not have finished the trip in one day. Also, considering that diesel is now nearly $4 per gallon, the Delorme route would have wasted 7 extra gallons of fuel (45 miles / 6.5 mpg) - at a cost of approximately $28. The Delorme product can be manually tweaked by "Via" points, but I shouldn't have to do this.

I returned the Delorme product (thanks, Amazon!), and bought Microsoft Streets and Trips instead. I personally find it more intuitive and easier to figure out than the Delorme product. I mapped the same trip (Sumner, WA --> Great Falls, MT) and it mapped it perfectly, using both WA-18 and MT-200.

Another advantage of the Microsoft product is the after-market work on the Points of Interest. If you Google "The Points of Interest Mega File," you'll see what I mean. They have added a LOT of trucker-friendly (and RV-friendly) information, such as Walmarts that allow parking, Costco, Sam's Club, Cracker Barrel restaurants, Rest stops in each state, etc - things that might not have been included in the original released version. Literally thousands of new entries. Nice!

The one complaint that I have about the Microsoft product - and the reason for the 4 stars instead of 5 - isthat the POIs don't include Churches in the "find nearby places" list. This was a surprise to me - especially considering some of the other rather obscure categories that were included. (The Delorme product did list Churches, but did not distinguish between denominations - it was a mess, but it was there.) The Microsoft product didn't list any Churches at all.

For instance, I created a category for Auto and I have subcategories for fuel, service, registration, and insurance.  Fuel and service charges happen when they happen, but registration and insurance are scheduled bills. I built a category group for regularly scheduled bills and one for non-recurring expenses (so I can trend my spend during any given month). When I run a budget report, the budget for the Auto category is broken into these two category groups (which is what I want), but the overall budget for Auto shows zero. I’ve been a Mac user for about 30 years. I’ve used Quicken successfully to run my small business (I’m the only employee) and my personal finances for 23 of those. “Successfully,” I’d say, until Quicken for Mac 2015. I was forced to upgrade Quicken when I recently upgraded my system to Yosemite.

Quicken 2015 for Mac is by far the worst program I have used in 30 years. Avoid it if you can. Here’s why.

For decades, Quicken was generally simple to use and understand. For my business account, I maintained standard ledgers—Accounts Receivable, Disbursements, Checking, etc. Money/assets moved smoothly from one account to the other. At the end of the year, I easily created and exported to Excel transaction reports that reflected in one tidy file all my financial activity for the year.

All that ended with Quicken for Mac 2015. Somebody at Intuit must have got the idea it needed a facelift . . . and turned it into a trophy wife: Pretty on the outside, empty head on the inside. I have rarely seen a program dumbed down so badly. It wasn’t broken, but they fixed it anyway.

First, transfer from my old Quicken took a day to get it to stop reimporting—thereby doubling, then tripling, then quadrupling my old accounts. Maybe they fixed that, maybe they didn’t.

Gone are the easy ledger transfers. They just don’t work any more. Try reducing your accounts receivable balance when the check comes in. No can do.

Reporting is extraordinarily limited. Customization and sorting is childishly narrow.

Want to export your reports to Excel? Sorry, not possible.

So where are all my saved transactions from the old Quicken (the ones you could select from a list)? Gone. You have to recreate them.

Out of the box it comes with some of the strangest preferences I have ever seen. A few hours with the barely adequate help screens plus some trial and error eventually got me where I need to go.

Reconciling accounts is as squirrely as they come. The old Quicken was simple, elegant, straightforward and easily understandable. Want to revisit a previous reconciliation? I have yet to figure out how to do it. It won’t let me.

Why did I give this two stars and not one? A few things worked as expected. And on the several times I turned to the community, I got prompt, courteous help (I’m guessing by Intuit plants), even when they had to tell me I was out of luck.

If you want flashy screens and pretty graphs Quicken for Mac 2015 is for you. Apparently, nobody knows how to budget money any more; they spend their time following their Quicken-tied stock investments instead. If that’s you, this version may be right up your alley. Maybe these features work, maybe they don’t. I’ve never used or tried them.

The ultimate clue to Quicken for Mac 2015’s awful performance came in a forum response declaring that “Quicken is not really set up for businesses.” That’s been false for 23 years. What the responder meant was Quicken for Mac 2015 has been altered from a previously business-friendly program to one that isn’t, in order to boost QuickBooks sales at $350 a pop.

I am planning to look for alternatives. There are a few out there. I will have to balance the usual pain of changing to and learning another program and the fear of importation of 23 years of financial information against the liberation from this dog. If you are looking for your first, do not overlook these other alternatives. Intuit has left a lot of us in the dust. You could be next.

This is a VERY limited photo editing program. It doesn't even do red-eye removal.  It's main claim, object removal, to put it bluntly, doesn't work.  The program has no idea what is supposed to fill the space where something is removed, so it merely stretches nearby objects, colors, etc., to fill the space with odd "junk."  It does have a clone stamp tool to manually fix its mess, but there is nothing like a smudge or blur tool to smooth out the fill.  Therefore, it is difficult to impossible to get a result with no sign of where the object was, as is claimed.  There are no other tools to allow one to get artistic, either.  It will add text to photos, in various sizes, fonts, and colors.  You can print the picture, but there are no print options.  There are far better photo editing programs available, some even free.

I've been using Norton Internet Security for many years, including the latest 2013 edition. For all of the bloat of the application, I always assumed that I was being protected from viruses and malware. It's the core reason for this software's existence.

For the past year, my computer was slowing down. A little at first - longer up times, longer software load times. Then this creeped into a more significant lag for all functions. Finally, last week, my laptop finally stopped responding. It's an HP DV9 with 1 TB hard drive space and 8 GB RAM, and a decent processor, so it should not have slowed given the workload I produce (standard business software). I brought it into my local PC repair, Geeks On Wheels (can't say enough about them), and they informed me that several very destructive viruses had infiltrated my PC. I told them that I run NIS regularly, at least weekly, and it monitors processes real-time. I also told them that I run Advanced Systemcare as an extra precaution and to help unclog my registries. They told me that Norton was one of their least favorite antivirus programs, because for all of it's size and scope, it has a poor record of virus detection and removal. Their recommendation was ESet Antivirus.

The cynical side of me assumed they were trying to make a buck on replacing my antivirus, so I conducted an experiment. I ran Norton on my other 3 laptops, a full system scan. Nothing was found on any of these. Then I downloaded the free trial of ESet Antivirus and ran it. In every case, ESet found multiple viruses and malware. In the case of my daughter's machine, it found 20! After each scan, all machines ran more quickly.

So, before spending a lot on NIS, try ESet. Do the same test I did. You won't spend a dime unless you decide to switch, and you might save yourself the pain of losing a machine for days as I did fixing the issues that NIS was supposed to prevent.

As a long time Photoshop user, I was looking for a competent replacement as I am no longer involved in a job role that mandates having access to the latest Adobe CC offering. Adobe CC is great---but I certainly don't need to spend $120 a year just for Photoshop and Lightroom ($10 a month for Adobe's lowest package offering), and there are competent replacements for the other Adobe products that don't require a subscription.

Having used some of Serif's products in the past and had a good experience, I took a chance on PhotoPlus X6, thinking that it should be able to duplicate most of what I was looking for.

For the projects I work on I am most interested in non-destructive filter and layer effects. In terms of the "raw" features I need, PhotoPlus X6 hits most of the major checkboxes---non-destructive effects for bevel, dropshadow, saturation, contrast, color balance; a reasonable assortment of brushes; ability to do fast and easy pattern stamping. The interface is mostly in the same vein as Photoshop, which is a plus, since it's what I'm used to, so I felt at home almost immediately using it.

As long as you approach your use of the program from a reasonably "casual" viewpoint, the app shines. Quick adjustments, a crop here or there, a minor content replacement there, and everything works and runs reasonably smoothly.

However, as soon as you start to push the envelope at all, things don't go so well. First, I wouldn't recommend attempting to do anything with images larger than 10 megapixels, simply due to the speed of the rendering engine. Simply put, images that I used to edit in Photoshop with dozens of layers and adjustments at 12 megapixel sizes simply chokes on PhotoPlus. Changing layer states, moving between tools, ANYTHING you do when working on large sized images with layers and effects takes 3-5 seconds just for the tools to respond.

Like I say, for simple, minimal adjustments the speed difference is negligible, but once you start adding on layers and effects, Photoshop quickly pulls ahead as the superior choice for speed.

For me the speed difference is by far the most troubling, but there's other niggles that get under my skin. One, there's no text on a path support, which I use extensively; you're basically limited to straight-line text. Two, the blur tool simply doesn't work in any way that feels intuitive compared to Photoshop. Photoshop's blur tool feels intuitive and "right" out of the box; I had to spend a good hour fiddling with the various tool settings to get PhotoPlus's to come anywhere close to it (and it still doesn't work right).

While Serif's non-destructive pattern/bump mapping layer effects can create some impressive visuals, doing something as simple a texture pattern overlay layer is an exercise in frustration.

All told, PhotoPlus X6 ends up being exactly what you'd expect from a company running from behind the market leader---for the price it's a decent piece of software, but it's nothing to rave about. The "big picture" features and tools are there and mostly work as intended, but moderate to power users will find themselves wistfully sighing for the elegance and usability that's missing.

I've been filing my own taxes for over a decade.  The tax code is definitely unwieldy and confusing, but I sat down and familiarized myself with it anyway.  I've used TurboTax, TaxAct and TaxCut, mostly TaxAct since it gives free Federal filing.  It's also less expensive than the others by a wide margin.  I decided to give TurboTax another chance to see if it could handle my tax requirements this year.    My first mistake was buying the Premier version instead of the Deluxe version.  Either I misread the description or it was changed after I bought it, because I could have sworn I saw 1 free State efile.  However the description says nothing of the sort now, and I have no way to verify what actually happened.  That's not a big deal, but what is a big deal is how this program does its error checking.  The issue is that TurboTax does not go over some of the extremely less common deductions - which are valid deductions - so you have to modify the form directly to add it in.  My largest deduction is a third of my annual income; that's not chump change.  Without that deduction I'd have to go to zero exemptions and still owe both governments money every year; screw that.  TaxAct asks the question, even though it's somewhat buried.  Don't know if TaxCut does, but it's probably a good bet that it doesn't.  Points for TaxAct here - until we get smart enough to pass FairTax, I have to suffer this robbery, so I need to make sure I get back what I'm owed, period.    So I mentioned about the State filing; there is an error check step near the end, and for mine it gave me a clean bill.  It also stated that I was low risk for audit, except for my business expenses as I use my car for work purposes...I've got all sorts of documentation for that, so no biggie (although, another negative about this later).  Problem is that it gets to the point of efiling, and it will bill you $20 before it will file the State.  AFTER billing you, it does another \\"more rigorous\\" check, and that's whenit will reject your efile...if you manually modify the form in any way, even if the program is overlooking critical deductions, it won't allow you to efile.  This is simply silly, because it does calculation verification earlier anyway; what's the point of this?    I sent an email to Intuit demanding my $20 back.  Haven't heard ne'er a word from them.  I imagine that money is Lost in Emotion...que sera, que sera.    The program is also spotty with its math.  I had to print the forms 4 separate times, because each time I'd go through it, I would look on the form and notice a critical oversight.  For example, I told it to import my 2008 data from TaxAct (a cool feature, mind you), but when it did, it imported blatantly wrong, and it didn't ask me to verify each piece of information that was imported.  It never pulled any of the financial data either, only my name, address, and exemption status, all of which were wrong.  It logged me as being subject to someone else claiming me as a dependent even though that was never the case; I was confused when I got to the Making Work Pay credit and having it tell me this even though it just wasn't true.  Then I went through and itemized my deductions; first it claimed that because my itemized deductions were significantly higher than the standard deduction that I should do that, resulting in a hefty refund.  After I printed the forms again, I noticed that I had overlooked two things; first, I had two business cars for the year, one of which was new.  It logged the New Car deduction properly, and it claimed I had over 50% business utilization.  The problem is, when I added the other car, which had just as many business miles as the new car, it treated them as separate for purposes of business use calculation.  Now maybe that's the tax code, I don't know, but together they still added up to over 50%, yet all of a sudden I was not eligible for these deductions and was forced to go back down to standard.  That was quite irritating.The refund is still high, but it dropped by a little over 1k because of that.    So, there you have it.  It's not a bad program if you have complex taxes to file, just know that unlike their claim, you're probably not getting all of the credits and deductions you should be getting.  If you aren't familiar with the tax code specific to your individual situation I suggest you get cracking on reading up about it, because if you don't, you won't know that you're missing out.  I also recommend TaxAct above this program, as while it's not as \\"pretty\\" as TurboTax, it goes into the nitty-gritty of your tax situation better to where you're maximizing the deductions and credits properly.

Example: I needed to reset the Windows 7 password on a friend's computer. She has an HP Pavilion. For about two seconds, that interrupt screen shows and gave me a choice to press [esc] to boot from a different device like the USB. So on her machine there was no pressing F2 as the computer gave me an option screen. So know your computer and know which device you're going to boot from. The program works.... if you take the time to understand your computer's boot sequence.

This does not apply to you if you only have one account on your Mac.  However if you run multiple users on the Mac read on, as you may have the problem described below.  A few years ago I documented installation problems H&R Block has when you run multi-user on Macs (which you should as a good security practice).  That review is here: [[ASIN:B002SR4S0Q H&R Block At Home 2009 Deluxe Federal + State + eFile [OLD VERSION]]]  Although it's better, there is still one problem that may be difficult or impossible for most non-techie sorts to figure out on their own.  It has to do with State program installation.  The problem and the solution is below:  I always install programs as root or Administrator to ensure file permissions are all OK.  (Indeed not doing so in past years caused problems with H&R Block).  Once installed (both the Federal and the State plug-in) I switch back to a normal non-privileged user to run all of my programs to include H&R Block.  The problem occurred when I wanted to start the state program. Although I had successfully downloaded and installed the state plug-in as root/Admin (in my case Maryland) when I tried to access it as my normal user it said I did not have a state program installed, and offered to let me buy one!  Here's how you have to solve the problem:  Sign back in as root/Admin.  Using the Finder navigate down to Library/Application Support/H&RBlock/H&RBlock 2011/Completed Updates/ then copy the file xx.TCstate11 where xx is the two-letter abbreviation for your state.  (In my case that was the MD.TCstate11 file).  Using Finder navigate to a shared directory that can be accessed by both users, e.g. Macintosh HD/Users/Shared and paste a copy of that file into that shared directory.  Go back to your normal user and sign in again.  Navigate to the Macintosh HD/Users/Shared directory and find your xx.TCstate11 file.  Using another Finder window navigate down to your home directory then the directory Library/Application Support/H&RBlock/H&RBlock 2011/Completed Updates/  (I had to create the Completed Updates directory in my normal user account as it did not exist yet).  Copy (or move) the xx.TCstate11 file into the directory above.  Double click that xx.TCstate11 file. A .dmg mountable file appears.  Double click on that too, and a state installer pop-up appears, which then redownloads your already-paid-for state program and inserts it as a plug-in to your normal user account library profile.  You're good to go.  This is annoying especially since I reported similar multi-user install problems in past years to H&R Block.  Apparently they still haven't gotten that bug worked out.  Sigh.  Anyway, this would be a five star review without that installation bug that affects some users, but two stars got deducted for not fixing a known flaw that has been known by them for two years.  (I called and wrote the company documenting it in addition to my Amazon reviews.)
